# Measure

`§0` stated the goal in numbers. `§24` says the site ships able to report them. This
file is what gets instrumented, how, and what Loop 8 does with it.

A site nobody measures cannot be improved, and every claim made about it afterward is
a guess — including the client's claim that the redesign worked and yours that it
did.

---

## 1. Before you change anything: the baseline

Recorded in Loop 1, from the existing site. Without it, Loop 8 has nothing to compare
against and the whole run becomes unfalsifiable.

| Metric | Where from | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Sessions / month, last 12 | Analytics | Seasonality, and the denominator for everything |
| Conversions / month, last 12 | Analytics or the CRM | The number in `§0` |
| Conversion rate | Both of the above | The thing the run is trying to move |
| Traffic by source | Analytics | A redesign changes organic and direct differently |
| Top 20 landing pages by sessions | Analytics | These are the pages that must not break (`§13`) |
| Top 20 queries by impressions and clicks | Search Console | The rankings at risk |
| Core Web Vitals, mobile | CrUX / Search Console | Field data, not lab |
| Average lead quality | Sales | The number that decides whether more leads is a win |

**Screenshot and export all of it into `runs/<slug>/baseline/`.** Analytics properties
get reconfigured, access gets lost, and a client who switches analytics vendors
during a redesign has destroyed their own comparison. This costs ten minutes and it
is the only thing that makes Loop 8 honest.

No analytics at all? That is a finding, not a blocker. Loop 5 installs measurement,
Loop 8 sets the baseline instead of beating one, and `REPORT.md` says so plainly.

## 2. What to install

One analytics property. Not three, and not two of the same kind because nobody
switched the old one off.

| Layer | What | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Analytics** | One product | Prefer cookieless and aggregate (`§16`). Consent-free measurement beats consented measurement that misses a large share of sessions |
| **Search Console** | Verified, sitemap submitted | Free, irreplaceable, and the only source of query data |
| **Conversion events** | One per action in `FUNNEL.md` | Named, deduplicated, documented |
| **Ad platform conversions** | Only if paid traffic runs | Server-side where possible. Consent-gated always |
| **Uptime check** | One | A site nobody monitors goes down on a Saturday and nobody notices until Monday |
| **Form delivery alert** | One | The `§18` failure mode is silent. An alert if zero submissions arrive in N days is the cheapest insurance in the pipeline |

Everything here is a third-party tag and is subject to `§15`: named owner, stated job,
loaded after consent and after first paint.

### What not to install

Heatmaps and session recorders on a permanent basis — run them for two weeks with a
question, then remove them. They are heavy, they see form contents, and they are a
privacy disclosure most clients have not made.

Tag managers "so marketing can add things later" — the thing marketing adds later
becomes the LCP problem nobody can trace. If the client insists, gate it behind
consent and review it at Loop 8.

Two analytics products so that "we can compare". They will disagree, and everyone
will spend a quarter arguing about which is right.

## 3. The event model

Keep it small enough that a human can hold it. A funnel of six events beats a taxonomy
of sixty that nobody queries.

| Event | Fires when | Properties |
|---|---|---|
| `page_view` | Automatic | path, referrer, utm_* |
| `cta_click` | Any primary CTA | location (hero / mid / sticky), label |
| `form_start` | First field focused | form_id |
| `form_submit` | Successful submission only | form_id, page |
| `form_error` | Validation or network failure | form_id, reason — **the most under-collected and most useful event on this list** |
| `conversion` | Once, on the confirmed action | type, value if known |
| `demo_booked` | Calendar confirms | slot, source |
| `outbound_click` | Docs, app login, app store | destination |

Rules:

- **Named consistently.** `snake_case`, verb_noun, same names across every page
- **Fire once.** A conversion that double-fires on a re-render corrupts the number and
  costs money on ad platforms. Loop 7 checks this specifically
- **Only on success.** A `form_submit` fired on button click, before the request
  resolves, counts every failure as a win — which means an entirely broken form
  reports 100% conversion
- **Documented in `FUNNEL.md`**, with the trigger and the property list, so the next
  person can extend it without inventing a parallel scheme

### UTMs

Agree one convention and write it in the handover: `utm_source`, `utm_medium`,
`utm_campaign`, lowercase, hyphenated, no spaces. Preserve them across internal
navigation so the conversion attributes to the campaign that paid for it. Strip them
from canonical URLs so they never fragment the analytics or the index.

### Attribution honesty

Last-click is the default and it is wrong, always, in a knowable direction: it
over-credits branded search and paid retargeting, and under-credits everything that
created the demand. Say so once in the report. Do not build a multi-touch model on
traffic this size; instead, ask new leads a single question in the form — "how did you
hear about us" belongs in the CRM's first sales email, never on the site (`CONVERSION.md`).

## 4. Verify the instrumentation — Loop 7

`funnel-verifier` runs this, live, and it is part of the `§18` hard rule.

1. Load a page with consent rejected. Confirm **no** analytics request goes out
2. Accept consent. Confirm exactly one page_view
3. Click the primary CTA. Confirm one `cta_click` with the right location
4. Start the form. Confirm one `form_start`
5. Submit a real, clearly labeled test lead
6. Confirm the success state renders and `form_submit` fires **once**
7. Confirm the lead arrives at every destination: CRM record, inbox, channel
8. Confirm the autoresponder sends and does not land in spam
9. Confirm the conversion event appears in the analytics property, not just in the
   network tab
10. Repeat the whole thing on mobile, and on the second-most-used browser
11. Trigger a form error deliberately and confirm `form_error` fires with a reason
12. Delete the test lead from the CRM, or label it so sales does not call it

Steps 7 and 8 cannot be done from the browser alone. The conductor confirms the far
end with the client — an agent watching a success message is not evidence the lead
arrived (`§18`).

## 5. Loop 8 — reading it

Runs after real traffic. Two weeks minimum for a directional read, four to six for
anything a client should act on, and longer for a low-traffic B2B site. Say which one
you have.

### The report

1. **The `§0` goal, against the baseline.** Sessions, conversions, conversion rate,
   before and after, with the date range and the caveats stated
2. **What moved and what didn't.** Traffic and rate move for different reasons; a
   redesign that doubled the rate on flat traffic is a different result from one that
   doubled traffic at the old rate
3. **The funnel, step by step.** Where people leave. The biggest drop is the next
   piece of work, and it is rarely where the client expects
4. **Search performance.** Rankings held or moved. Any 404 or crawl error since
   launch. Redirect map still resolving
5. **Core Web Vitals in field data**, which will disagree with the lab number from
   Loop 7. Field data wins
6. **Lead quality from sales**, not just lead count. More leads of worse quality is a
   loss, and only sales can tell you

### Confounders, stated plainly

A redesign is never a clean experiment. Seasonality, a pricing change, a competitor's
campaign, a Google update, a sales hire — any of them can dominate the numbers.
Attributing everything to the site is how agencies lose clients in month three.

Name the confounders you can see. Where the result is genuinely ambiguous, say so.
Honest ambiguity survives a board meeting; a confident wrong attribution does not.

### Then propose the next three things

Ranked by expected impact against effort, each with the number it should move and how
you would know. Take them from the drop-off, not from taste. `CONVERSION.md §9` ranks
the usual levers — and the offer's rung on the friction ladder is nearly always the
biggest one nobody has tested.

## 6. Hand the numbers over

The client should be able to open a dashboard and see the goal number without asking
you. Deliver:

- Access to the analytics property, owned by them, on their account (`§23`)
- One saved view or dashboard showing exactly the `§0` metric over time
- `FUNNEL.md`, which documents every event and where it fires
- A one-page "how to read this" in their repository, in their words, naming the one
  number that matters and what a bad week looks like

A dashboard only you can read is another dependency (`§21`).

## Skip cost

Skipping measurement means the run cannot be evaluated. The site may be better or
worse and nobody will ever know, the client's next agency will start from the same
blank page, and every claim about the redesign becomes a matter of opinion.

It also removes Loop 8 entirely, which is where the compounding value of this pipeline
lives — the first version is a hypothesis, and the second one is where it starts
paying.

input.content:
# Architecture

How many pages the site has, how they route, and — the part that gets skipped — who
changes the pricing page on a Tuesday when you are not available.

Decided at **Gate A**, before any design work, because it changes the stack, the
build, the SEO surface, and the deploy adapter. Deciding it at build time means
rebuilding.

---

## The four shapes

| Shape | When it's right | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Landing page** | One offer, one audience, paid traffic or a launch. No navigation to speak of | Cheapest. One artifact, heavily instrumented, iterated against a number |
| **Small marketing site** | 4–8 pages, no publishing cadence, content changes a few times a year | Routing, per-page meta, real nav |
| **Marketing site + blog / resources** | They publish, or genuinely intend to | A generator with content collections |
| **Marketing site + CMS** | A non-technical marketing team owns the words and changes them weekly | A generator plus a headless CMS, or a platform with one |

Default to the smallest shape the client's actual behavior supports. A CMS built for
a team that edits twice a year is machinery nobody learns to use, and it rots.

### The honest question

Ask who will change this, how often, and what they will change. Then ask what they
did to their current site in the last six months. The second answer is the real one.

| They said | They actually did | Build for |
|---|---|---|
| "We'll blog weekly" | Two posts in two years | No blog. Say so |
| "We rarely change anything" | Six pricing edits and a launch banner | CMS or at least an editable content layer |
| "Marketing owns the site" | Every change went through a developer | Fix that. It is usually the highest-value thing in the run |

## Which pages exist

Not a template. Derived from the message hierarchy in `POSITIONING.md`, the objection
ladder, the buying committee, and the search intent map in `SEO.md`.

| Page | Exists when |
|---|---|
| **Home** | Always. Its job is to route, not to say everything |
| **Product / service** | One per genuinely distinct offering. Not one per feature |
| **Pricing** | Anything with a price. Even a band beats nothing (`CONVERSION.md`) |
| **Case studies** | Real ones exist and are cleared (`§25`). One deep beats six thin |
| **About** | Trust objection ranks high, or the founders are the differentiator |
| **Comparison / alternatives** | A named competitor dominates the search results. High intent, chronically missing |
| **Vertical or use-case pages** | Distinct segments with distinct triggers and distinct search demand |
| **Security / trust** | The buying committee includes security. A page the champion forwards |
| **Docs / API** | Developers evaluate before buying |
| **Careers** | They are hiring, and it is a real cost centre in their year |
| **Blog / resources** | They publish |
| **Contact** | Always, even when the primary path is a form elsewhere |
| **Legal** | Per [`COMPLIANCE.md`](./COMPLIANCE.md), driven by market and sector |

**Every page is a maintenance liability.** A page nobody updates and nobody visits
dilutes the site and eventually says something false. Cut on the way in.

### Vertical pages, and how they go wrong

Templated vertical pages — same page, industry noun swapped — are the classic
scale-fast mistake. They are thin, they compete with each other, and they read as
generated because they are. Build a vertical page only when there is a genuinely
different trigger, a different objection, and different proof. Three real ones beat
thirty templated ones.

## Routing

Flat and readable. The URL is part of the design and part of the ranking.

```
/                          home
/product  or /platform     the thing
/product/<feature>         only if a feature carries its own search intent
/pricing
/customers                 index
/customers/<slug>          case study
/compare/<competitor>      comparison pages
/for/<segment>             vertical or use-case
/about  /careers  /contact
/security                  trust page
/blog  /blog/<slug>
/legal/privacy  /legal/terms
```

Rules: no `/index.html` in a public URL, trailing slashes consistent and enforced by
one redirect, slugs lowercase and hyphenated, and **slugs never change once
published** — see `§13`. If one must change, it gets a 301 in `redirects.csv`.

Keep it under three clicks from home to any page that matters, and make sure the
comparison and vertical pages are linked from somewhere real, not orphaned behind a
sitemap.

## Navigation

`§3` applies: invent it for this client rather than reaching for a top bar with seven
items by reflex. Whatever it is, it satisfies the non-negotiables — keyboard
reachable, current page indicated, works at 360px, present on every page, and the
primary CTA visible without a scroll.

Two things that are almost always wrong on company sites, and worth fixing by
default:

- **A mega-menu on a nine-page site.** It exists because the client wants every page
  represented. Cut the nav to the pages that serve the decision, and let the footer
  carry the rest
- **The nav CTA and the page CTA being the same weight.** Nav is for the returning
  visitor. The page's ask is for the new one

The footer is where the long tail lives — legal, careers, secondary pages, company
details required by law (`COMPLIANCE.md`), and the small attribution from `§27`.

## The stack consequence

`PRINCIPLES.md` defaults to hand-authored HTML and CSS with committed assets. It runs
on all nine deploy targets and it is the fastest thing that can be built.

| Shape | Stack |
|---|---|
| Landing page | Hand-authored |
| Small marketing site | Hand-authored, or a generator if page count makes shared layout the bottleneck |
| Blog / resources | A generator with markdown content collections. Astro is the default: static output, no framework shipped by default, survives every deploy target |
| CMS | Generator plus a headless CMS, with a build hook. Or a platform that bundles both |

A generator is a build-time tool. The output is still static, still deployable
anywhere, and still under the `§19` budget. Using one does not mean shipping a
framework to the browser, and shipping a framework to the browser for a marketing
site is nearly always a mistake — it is the single most common reason a company site
fails Core Web Vitals.

### When SSR is genuinely warranted

Rare on marketing sites. Legitimate reasons: personalization the business actually
uses, a live pricing calculator hitting a private API, gated content with real
authentication, or a preview environment for CMS editors. "We might need it later" is
not one of them, and the cost is a server to keep alive and a whole class of failure
modes a static file does not have.

## The CMS decision

The question is not which CMS. It is **what the client edits, and what they must not
be able to break**.

| They edit | Give them |
|---|---|
| Blog posts only | Content collection in the repo, or a lightweight git-backed CMS |
| Copy on existing pages | A headless CMS with typed fields per section |
| Adding whole new pages | A page builder with locked components, or accept they will call you |
| Nothing, realistically | No CMS. Say it plainly and put the effort into the pages |

Whatever it is: **typed fields, not a rich-text blob.** A free-form WYSIWYG on a

rebuilding.

| Shape | When it's right | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Landing page** | One offer, one audience, paid traffic or a launch. No navigation to speak of | Cheapest. One artifact, heavily instrumented, iterated against a number |
| **Small marketing site** | 4–8 pages, no publishing cadence, content changes a few times a year | Routing, per-page meta, real nav |
| **Marketing site + blog / resources** | They publish, or genuinely intend to | A generator with content collections |
| **Marketing site + CMS** | A non-technical marketing team owns the words and changes them weekly | A generator plus a headless CMS, or a platform with one |

a team that edits twice a year is machinery nobody learns to use, and it rots.

Ask who will change this, how often, and what they will change. Then ask what they
did to their current site in the last six months. The second answer is the real one.

| They said | They actually did | Build for |

ladder, the buying committee, and the search intent map in `SEO.md`.

| **Product / service** | One per genuinely distinct offering. Not one per feature |
| **Pricing** | Anything with a price. Even a band beats nothing (`CONVERSION.md`) |
| **Case studies** | Real ones exist and are cleared (`§25`). One deep beats six thin |
| **About** | Trust objection ranks high, or the founders are the differentiator |
| **Comparison / alternatives** | A named competitor dominates the search results. High intent, chronically missing |
| **Vertical or use-case pages** | Distinct segments with distinct triggers and distinct search demand |
| **Security / trust** | The buying committee includes security. A page the champion forwards |
| **Docs / API** | Developers evaluate before buying |
| **Careers** | They are hiring, and it is a real cost centre in their year |
| **Blog / resources** | They publish |
| **Contact** | Always, even when the primary path is a form elsewhere |
| **Legal** | Per [`COMPLIANCE.md`](./COMPLIANCE.md), driven by market and sector |

**Every page is a maintenance liability.** A page nobody updates and nobody visits
dilutes the site and eventually says something false. Cut on the way in.

### Vertical pages, and how they go wrong

Templated vertical pages — same page, industry noun swapped — are the classic
scale-fast mistake. They are thin, they compete with each other, and they read as
generated because they are. Build a vertical page only when there is a genuinely
different trigger, a different objection, and different proof. Three real ones beat
thirty templated ones.

## Routing

Flat and readable. The URL is part of the design and part of the ranking.

```
/                          home
/product  or /platform     the thing
/product/<feature>         only if a feature carries its own search intent
/pricing
/customers                 index
/customers/<slug>          case study
/compare/<competitor>      comparison pages
/for/<segment>             vertical or use-case
/about  /careers  /contact
/security                  trust page
/blog  /blog/<slug>
/legal/privacy  /legal/terms
```

Rules: no `/index.html` in a public URL, trailing slashes consistent and enforced by
one redirect, slugs lowercase and hyphenated, and **slugs never change once
published** — see `§13`. If one must change, it gets a 301 in `redirects.csv`.

comparison and vertical pages are linked from somewhere real, not orphaned behind a
sitemap.

## Navigation

`§3` applies: invent it for this client rather than reaching for a top bar with seven
items by reflex. Whatever it is, it satisfies the non-negotiables — keyboard
reachable, current page indicated, works at 360px, present on every page, and the
primary CTA visible without a scroll.

default:

- **A mega-menu on a nine-page site.** It exists because the client wants every page
  represented. Cut the nav to the pages that serve the decision, and let the footer
  carry the rest
- **The nav CTA and the page CTA being the same weight.** Nav is for the returning
  visitor. The page's ask is for the new one

| Shape | Stack |
|---|---|

A generator is a build-time tool. The output is still static, still deployable
anywhere, and still under the `§19` budget. Using one does not mean shipping a
framework to the browser, and shipping a framework to the browser for a marketing
site is nearly always a mistake — it is the single most common reason a company site
fails Core Web Vitals.

| They edit | Give them |

# Styles

What it looks like. Thirty starting positions, what each one signals to a buyer, and
what it costs.

`§3` is the rule that governs this file: these are a **starting position, never a
destination**. Ship a named style unmodified and the run failed. Every entry below is
something to collide, subvert, or push past — the collision table and the subversion
section are the actual work.

The commercial difference from a personal site: a style here is read as a claim about
the company. A visitor decides whether this looks like a business that can handle
their contract before reading a word, and they are not wrong to. Style choice is a
trust decision as much as a taste one.

---

## Picking one

The style shortlist comes from the translation table in `BRIEF.md`, not from taste:

1. **Category cluster** (`POSITIONING.md §5`) — what every competitor already looks
   like. That is the fence, not the field
2. **The empty position** — what nobody in the category looks like, that this client
   could credibly be
3. **Anti-positioning** — styles banned outright. Honor absolutely
4. **The buyer's risk appetite** — a procurement committee buying infrastructure and
   a founder buying a design sprint tolerate different amounts of strangeness
5. **What the brand already owns** (`POSITIONING.md §12`) — load-bearing elements are
   constraints, not suggestions

Never one answer. Bring three families to Gate B1 (`§4`).

---

## Authority and institutional

Styles that say *this company will still exist in five years*. Reach for these when
the ranking objection is trust, when the contract is large, or when the buyer is a
committee.

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Swiss / International** | Strict grid, one grotesk, generous whitespace, flush-left everything | Rigor, seriousness, engineering culture | The most crowded style in B2B. Unmodified, it is invisible |
| **Editorial** | Magazine structure: measure, drop caps, marginalia, pull quotes, a real type hierarchy | Thoughtfulness, expertise, something worth reading | Wants real copy. Fails hard with placeholder-length text |
| **Corporate modernist** | Institutional grotesk, restrained palette, photography as evidence | Scale and permanence | Slides into the beige default if nothing is pushed |
| **Archival / documentary** | Records, dates, indexes, tabular listings, serif captions | A body of work that exists and was catalogued | Needs actual volume. Thin content reads as pretension |
| **Blueprint / technical drawing** | Line weights, dimension rules, annotation callouts, hairline grid | Precision. Excellent for anything engineered or manufactured | Reads cold. Pair with warmth somewhere |
| **Legal-formal** | Justified columns, small caps, footnotes, near-monochrome | Gravity, discretion, professional service | Almost no room for delight. Deliberate choice only |

## Product and clarity

Styles built to make software legible. The register of most SaaS marketing, which is
exactly why the unmodified versions are the least distinguishing choice available.

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Product-first** | The real UI at working resolution, annotated, carrying the page | Confidence — the product is the argument (`§11`) | Only as good as the UI. Ugly product, honest problem |
| **Bento** | Modular tiles of varying size, each carrying one idea | Feature breadth without a wall of text | The most imitated layout of the decade. Unmodified it dates the site instantly |
| **Diagrammatic** | The page explains a system: flows, nodes, before-and-after | Comprehension for anything with a non-obvious mechanism | Needs a real diagram, not decoration with arrows |
| **Dashboard-native** | Marketing site borrowing the product's own visual language | Continuity from site to trial | Confusing when the site and product diverge later |
| **Comparison-led** | The page is a table, and the table is the argument | Fearlessness, when the client genuinely wins | Legal exposure (`COMPLIANCE.md`). Every cell is a claim |
| **Instructional** | Numbered steps, worked example, real data | Removes the switching-cost objection by showing the work | Long. Earn the scroll |

## Craft and material

Styles that make a page feel made rather than assembled. Strong for agencies, studios,
and premium positioning where the work itself is the product.

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Risograph / print artifact** | Misregistration, limited spot inks, halftone, paper grain | A hand and a press. Warmth, craft, a physical object | Reads indie. Wrong for enterprise infrastructure |
| **Letterpress / debossed** | Physical impression, subtle relief, ink spread | Heritage and permanence | Contrast traps. See the accessibility table |
| **Collage** | Cut edges, mixed media, overlapping registration, deliberate mess | Creative capability, editorial voice | Hard to keep legible and harder to keep on-brand across pages |
| **Ink and gesture** | Brush strokes, wet edges, one human mark against structure | A person made a decision here | One gesture. Two is decoration |
| **Textile / material substrate** | Weave, fibre, stitched edges, tactile fills | Handmade, sustainable, physical-goods brands | Heavy assets unless generated (`§14`, `CRAFT.md`) |
| **Photographic-led** | Real photography carrying the design, type as a quiet layer | Reality, scale, people | Only with real, licensed, non-stock photography. Otherwise it is the laughing-at-a-laptop failure |

## Atmosphere and depth

Styles with a mood. Effective for premium positioning and for products whose value is
felt rather than enumerated. Dangerous when the buyer needs to read a spec.

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cinematic dark** | Single key light, deep falloff, grade, grain, vignette | Premium, considered, high production value | Contrast discipline required. Body copy suffers in the falloff |
| **Aurora / mesh gradient** | Soft multi-stop fields, slow drift | Depth and modernity at almost no cost | **The single most exhausted style in SaaS.** Only heavily subverted |
| **Glass / refractive** | Blur, refraction, layered translucency, real depth | Sophistication, layered systems | Text contrast changes with what scrolls behind it |
| **Spatial / 3D world** | A navigable scene with depth and camera | Ambition, and a product with a physical or spatial dimension | Expensive, and a fallback is mandatory (`§17`) |
| **Volumetric light** | Rays, participating media, atmosphere | Air in the scene. Turns flat into a place | Easy to overcook into a stock render |
| **Nocturne** | Near-black substrate, one saturated accent, high restraint | Focus. Everything else falls away | Every element must earn its light |

## Structural and typographic

Styles where the layout and the type *are* the design. Cheap to build, fast, and
frequently the strongest differentiator available in a category full of gradients.

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Radical minimalism** | Almost nothing. One idea per screen, enormous whitespace | Confidence. Nothing to hide behind | Only works with a genuinely strong message. Weak copy is naked here |
| **Typographic-led** | Type at display scale doing the work of imagery | Voice, editorial confidence, zero asset weight | Needs a real type system and real headline writing |
| **Brutalist / raw** | Exposed structure, system fonts, unstyled defaults made deliberate | Anti-marketing honesty. Strong for developer tools | Reads as unfinished to a non-technical buyer |
| **Neo-brutalist** | Hard borders, flat shadows, clashing color, oversized controls | Energy, irreverence, a challenger stance | Now a template of its own. Requires real subversion |
| **Grid-broken** | An established grid, deliberately violated at chosen moments | Control — you only break a rule you can keep | Random-looking if the underlying grid is not visible first |
| **Modular scale-extreme** | Enormous ratio between display and body | Hierarchy you can read across a room | Mobile needs a separate scale, not a scaled-down one |
| **Terminal / monospace** | Fixed cells, monospace, command-line register | Native credibility with developers | Instantly wrong for anyone who is not one |

## Motion-native and interactive

Styles where the behavior is the design. Powerful and expensive, and each one needs
its designed reduced-motion state (`§17`).

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scroll-cinema** | Scroll as scrub head; the page is a sequence the visitor drives | Narrative control, high production value | Hostile to skimmers, and buyers skim. Never on a pricing page |
| **Kinetic typography** | Words as the animated subject | Voice, energy, memorability | Slow to read. Headline only |
| **Physics / spring world** | Elements with weight, inertia, collision | Playfulness, a product that feels responsive | Novelty wears off in eight seconds. It cannot carry a page |
| **Interactive demo-led** | The hero *is* the product, usable without signup | The strongest conversion move available (`CONVERSION.md`) | Real engineering, and a maintenance liability |
| **Data-live** | Real numbers from the real system, moving | Proof rendered as motion. Rank 1 or 2, made visible | Needs an endpoint, and a designed state for when it is down |
| **Cursor-driven** | The pointer reveals, distorts, or lights the page | A designed environment, within one second | Mobile has no cursor. Design that case first, not last |

## Category clichés — the fence, not the field

What the visitor has already seen five times this morning. `§2` and `§3` mean these
are not available unmodified. Check the client's category before Gate B1.

| Category | The cliché | Why it persists | The opening |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B2B SaaS** | Purple-to-blue gradient, isometric illustration, centered hero, three cards, logo bar | Every template ships it | Real product UI (`§11`), editorial structure, visible pricing |
| **Agency / studio** | Full-bleed dark video, oversized rotating type, a horizontal case-study rail, a cursor dot | It signals membership in the agency club | Work at depth, the process, a stated refusal, actual results with numbers |
| **AI product** | Purple glow, particle mesh, gradient orb, "powered by AI", a chat bubble | The category is 20 months old and copies itself | Show the output. The demo is the differentiator, and almost nobody ships one |
| **Fintech** | Blue, a phone mockup at an angle, abstract nodes, a padlock icon | Trust-by-convention | Real numbers, real regulation named, real screens |
| **Developer tool** | Dark terminal hero, a code block, monospace everything | Native credibility, and now noise | Show the failure it prevents. Benchmark honestly. Docs as the marketing site |
| **Healthcare** | Stock clinician, soft blue-green, rounded everything, hands | Regulatory caution flattened into blandness | Specificity about the condition, the workflow, the outcome |
| **Ecommerce brand** | Hero lifestyle shot, three-up product grid, a countdown bar | Platform themes | Product at obsessive resolution, the making, the material |
| **Professional services** | Handshake photo, a serif wordmark, "trusted advisors" | Risk aversion | Named people, named outcomes, an opinion someone could disagree with |
| **Local service** | Template with a stock van, five-star widget, a phone number in a banner | Whoever built it charged £400 | Real photos of real work, a real person, real prices |

Being the only site in the category that shows a price, ships a working demo, or
names a person is worth more than any visual move on this page.

---

## Collision

`§3` in practice. Two styles, one carrying structure and one carrying surface,
producing something neither has alone. Every run states its collision in one sentence
in `DIRECTION.md`.

| Collision | What it produces that neither parent has |
|---|---|
| **Editorial structure over live product data** | Magazine columns and a real measure, with the numbers inside them pulled from the running system. The article makes an argument and the argument updates itself, so the proof is not a screenshot of a claim but the claim still being true |
| **Blueprint substrate under photographic product shots** | The dimension rules and callouts assert measurement; the photograph asserts the thing exists. Together they read as a specification of a real object, which is what a manufacturing buyer is actually looking for |
| **Risograph texture on a Swiss grid** | The grid asserts machine order, the misregistration asserts a press and a hand. It reads as a printed object rather than a rendered page, and the grid stops looking like every other B2B site because it is visibly ink |
| **Terminal chrome around a physics world** | Monospace frames promise determinism and fixed cells; the contents obey springs and collide. A frame that cannot bend around contents that will not sit still is the whole idea |
| **Archival index with cinematic case-study reveals** | The list is a dry catalogue with dates and reference numbers; opening one drops into a graded, lit scene. The restraint of the index makes the reveal cost something |
| **Brutalist structure with a luxury type system** | Raw exposed layout and system-font honesty, set in a licensed high-contrast serif at enormous scale. The tension says expensive and unpretentious at once, which is exactly what a good agency is |
| **Radical minimalism holding one interactive demo** | An almost empty page whose single object is the working product. Nothing competes with it, so the demo carries the entire argument (`§11`) |
| **Instructional layout in a nocturne palette** | Numbered steps and worked examples, lit like a darkroom. Teaching without the classroom register that makes senior buyers feel handled |
| **Data-brutalism with one ink gesture** | Dense tabular numbers with a single brush stroke across them. The gesture asserts a person read these and had a view, which a table cannot say and a painting cannot evidence |
| **Diagrammatic system over textile substrate** | Nodes and flows on woven material. For anything bridging software and physical goods, it says both without a split-screen |

Rule for building one: **name which parent is structural and which is surface.** A
collision where both fight for structure is a mess, and it is the most common way this
technique fails.

## Subversion

The other route to `§3`. Take one style and break exactly one of its laws.

| Style | Its law | The subversion |
|---|---|---|
| Swiss | The grid is never violated | Violate it once, on the one section carrying the offer. The violation becomes the CTA |
| Radical minimalism | Nothing is decorated | One object, obsessively rendered, in an otherwise empty page |
| Bento | Tiles are equal citizens | One tile is thirty times the size of the others and contains the product |
| Cinematic dark | Everything is graded | One section is a flat, bright, unstyled document. The contrast reads as candor |
| Brutalist | Nothing is designed | The type is impeccable. Raw layout, perfect typography |
| Editorial | Text is the content | The article's illustrations are live, interactive, and manipulable |
| Terminal | Monospace, fixed grid | The body copy is a humanist serif at a generous measure. Technical frame, human voice |

# Styles

What it looks like. Thirty starting positions, what each one signals to a buyer, and
what it costs.

`§3` is the rule that governs this file: these are a **starting position, never a
destination**. Ship a named style unmodified and the run failed. Every entry below is
something to collide, subvert, or push past — the collision table and the subversion
section are the actual work.

The commercial difference from a personal site: a style here is read as a claim about
the company. A visitor decides whether this looks like a business that can handle
their contract before reading a word, and they are not wrong to. Style choice is a
trust decision as much as a taste one.

---

## Picking one

The style shortlist comes from the translation table in `BRIEF.md`, not from taste:

1. **Category cluster** (`POSITIONING.md §5`) — what every competitor already looks
   like. That is the fence, not the field
2. **The empty position** — what nobody in the category looks like, that this client
   could credibly be
3. **Anti-positioning** — styles banned outright. Honor absolutely
4. **The buyer's risk appetite** — a procurement committee buying infrastructure and
   a founder buying a design sprint tolerate different amounts of strangeness
5. **What the brand already owns** (`POSITIONING.md §12`) — load-bearing elements are
   constraints, not suggestions

Never one answer. Bring three families to Gate B1 (`§4`).

---

## Authority and institutional

Styles that say *this company will still exist in five years*. Reach for these when
the ranking objection is trust, when the contract is large, or when the buyer is a
committee.

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Swiss / International** | Strict grid, one grotesk, generous whitespace, flush-left everything | Rigor, seriousness, engineering culture | The most crowded style in B2B. Unmodified, it is invisible |
| **Editorial** | Magazine structure: measure, drop caps, marginalia, pull quotes, a real type hierarchy | Thoughtfulness, expertise, something worth reading | Wants real copy. Fails hard with placeholder-length text |
| **Corporate modernist** | Institutional grotesk, restrained palette, photography as evidence | Scale and permanence | Slides into the beige default if nothing is pushed |
| **Archival / documentary** | Records, dates, indexes, tabular listings, serif captions | A body of work that exists and was catalogued | Needs actual volume. Thin content reads as pretension |
| **Blueprint / technical drawing** | Line weights, dimension rules, annotation callouts, hairline grid | Precision. Excellent for anything engineered or manufactured | Reads cold. Pair with warmth somewhere |
| **Legal-formal** | Justified columns, small caps, footnotes, near-monochrome | Gravity, discretion, professional service | Almost no room for delight. Deliberate choice only |

## Product and clarity

Styles built to make software legible. The register of most SaaS marketing, which is
exactly why the unmodified versions are the least distinguishing choice available.

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Product-first** | The real UI at working resolution, annotated, carrying the page | Confidence — the product is the argument (`§11`) | Only as good as the UI. Ugly product, honest problem |
| **Bento** | Modular tiles of varying size, each carrying one idea | Feature breadth without a wall of text | The most imitated layout of the decade. Unmodified it dates the site instantly |
| **Diagrammatic** | The page explains a system: flows, nodes, before-and-after | Comprehension for anything with a non-obvious mechanism | Needs a real diagram, not decoration with arrows |
| **Dashboard-native** | Marketing site borrowing the product's own visual language | Continuity from site to trial | Confusing when the site and product diverge later |
| **Comparison-led** | The page is a table, and the table is the argument | Fearlessness, when the client genuinely wins | Legal exposure (`COMPLIANCE.md`). Every cell is a claim |
| **Instructional** | Numbered steps, worked example, real data | Removes the switching-cost objection by showing the work | Long. Earn the scroll |

Styles that make a page feel made rather than assembled. Strong for agencies, studios,
and premium positioning where the work itself is the product.

| Style | What it is | Signals | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|

| **Ink and gesture** | Brush strokes, wet edges, one human mark against structure | A person made a decision here | One gesture. Two is decoration |
| **Textile / material substrate** | Weave, fibre, stitched edges, tactile fills | Handmade, sustainable, physical-goods brands | Heavy assets unless generated (`§14`, `CRAFT.md`) |
| **Photographic-led** | Real photography carrying the design, type as a quiet layer | Reality, scale, people | Only with real, licensed, non-stock photography. Otherwise it is the laughing-at-a-laptop failure |

felt rather than enumerated. Dangerous when the buyer needs to read a spec.

# Craft

How you render it. `STYLES.md` decides what it looks like; this decides what it is
made of.

The mandate is `§2` and `§3`: advanced technique is the floor, not the ceiling. Look
anything up. Pull any library via CDN while prototyping. Build things this pipeline
has never built. The arsenal below is a starting position.

Three rules hold it honest, and they are the same three every loop enforces:

1. **Every technique gets a runnable prototype** before the design depends on it
   (Loop 2b). A technique that fails in a prototype is cut cheaply; the same failure
   in Loop 4 costs a rebuild.
2. **Every technique ships three states** — full, designed reduced-motion, and a
   no-WebGL or no-JS fallback (`§17`).
3. **Name the thing this technique makes the buyer understand.** No answer means
   remove it. On a company site the bar is higher than on a portfolio: impressive and
   irrelevant is not neutral, it is scroll depth the converting section needed.

And one that is specific to this pipeline: **the technique never delays the ask.**
Everything heavy lazy-loads after first paint and outside the LCP path (`§19`).

---

## The commercial test

Before any technique goes in `DIRECTION.md`, answer three questions in one line each:

| Question | Failure |
|---|---|
| What does this make the visitor **understand**? | "It looks impressive" — cut it |
| Which **objection** does it answer, or which **proof** does it carry? | None — demote it to a decorative layer with a byte budget |
| What does it cost in **bytes and main-thread time**? | Unknown — prototype it before it enters the design |

A technique that answers all three is worth building at any complexity. One that
answers none is worth nothing at any complexity.

---

## The arsenal

### Showing the product

The highest-value group on a company site (`§11`), and the most neglected.

| Technique | What it is | Where it earns its place |
|---|---|---|
| Live embedded product | The real application, running, in an iframe or a sandbox | The strongest conversion asset that exists. Rung 0–1 on the friction ladder |
| Scripted interactive demo | A faithful clickable replica driven by a script, not the real backend | When the real product needs auth or data. Much cheaper to maintain than it looks, and far better than video |
| Annotated UI crop | Real screen, cropped to one job, with callouts | Explains a mechanism in one screen. Works in email and in a deck too |
| Sequenced UI reveal | Screens stepping through a workflow on scroll or a timer | Shows a flow without a video's weight. Ship a paused, stepped fallback |
| Before / after scrubber | Draggable divider between two real states | Instantly legible proof for anything visual: migrations, cleanups, redesigns |
| Live data from the real system | A number, a chart, or a status pulled from production | Turns a rank-1 claim into something the visitor watches be true. Needs a designed offline state |
| Synthetic-data replica | The real UI, populated with realistic, non-real records | The answer when the product is under NDA or the data is personal (`§25`) |
| Video of the real thing | A real screen recording, short, poster-first, click to play | Never autoplay with sound. Poster image in the shell, player loaded on interaction |

**Never fake a screen that implies a feature that does not exist** (`§6`). A mocked-up
UI is allowed only when labeled as a concept, and on a marketing site it almost never
should be.

### Rendering and GPU

| Technique | What it is | Where it earns its place |
|---|---|---|
| Raymarching + SDFs | Geometry as a distance function, marched per pixel | A hero form that could not be modeled. Infinite repetition, soft shadows, ambient occlusion free |

return per byte on a commercial site:

6. **A 12-second real screen recording, poster-first**
7. **Named, faced, sourced proof placed next to the claim it supports**
8. **A form that is three fields and works** (`§18`)
9. **Print stylesheet and a proper OG image** — both invisible until someone needs them
10. **One collision-carrying signature moment**, prototyped, that no competitor has

Loop 2b, one agent per technique, in `runs/<slug>/prototypes/`.

at Loop 4, where everything gets downloaded, vendored, and committed (`§14`).

Each prototype delivers: a standalone runnable HTML file, a screenshot, a measured
frame rate under load on throttled hardware, the byte cost, and all three states.

cheap here is the entire point of the loop.

  path. It declares its number at Gate B2

  LCP element
- Every third-party tag deferred and consented (`§15`, `§16`)
- No layout shift after paint. Reserve space for everything that arrives late,
  including the cookie banner
- Measure on a throttled mid-range Android, not on the machine you built it on

A technique that cannot be deferred has to justify its bytes at Gate B2, in front of
the client, against the conversion goal.

| **Fallback** | No WebGL, no JS, old GPU, blocked script. A real page, never an apology |

is also a commercial one, because the visitor on locked-down corporate hardware with
scripts restricted is frequently the enterprise buyer.

# Models

Which tier of model runs which step, and who decides.

Running every loop on the best available model works and wastes a lot of it. Running
every loop on the cheapest produces a site that reads like it. Neither is the answer,
and the split is not where most people put it.

## The principle

**Tier follows the cost of being wrong, not the position in the pipeline.**

A step where a mistake is caught by the next command is cheap to get wrong. A step
whose output every later loop consumes is expensive to get wrong, and no amount of
downstream quality repairs it.

Three questions place any step:

1. **Is there a right answer a check could confirm?** Yes means low tier. Crawling a
   sitemap, building a redirect map, vendoring a library, running axe, checking that
   an event fired — all have right answers.
2. **Is there a spec, and does the work follow it?** Yes means mid tier. Coding to an
   approved design image, charting competitors against a fixed rubric, drafting a
   page to an approved message hierarchy.
3. **Does it require taste, synthesis, or reading a human?** Yes means top tier. No
   exceptions for time pressure, because this is the work that cannot be redone
   cheaply later.

## Where the intuition misleads

The natural instinct is cheap-early, expensive-late: discovery is just gathering,
design is where it gets hard. That is backwards here.

**The intake and the positioning are the most expensive steps in this pipeline to get
wrong.** Everything later consumes `BRIEF.md`. A shallow intake produces eight
shallow loops. Specifically, three judgments happen early and cannot be repaired
downstream:

- **Hearing the goal underneath the stated goal.** A client says "we need a
  redesign"; the real constraint is a board meeting in March and a sales team that
  cannot forward anything. Catching that changes the whole run
- **Reading the competitive chart.** The data is mechanical; knowing which empty
  position is defensible and which is empty for a good reason is not
- **The headline.** One line, derived from customer language, positioning, and the
  top objection at once. It is the highest-leverage sentence on the site and it is
  synthesis, not drafting

What is genuinely mechanical early on is the **crawl, the redirect map, the scrape,
and the review mining**. Those belong at the bottom tier and they run in parallel with
the intake anyway.

## The map

Tiers are named rather than versioned so this file does not rot.

| Tier | Today | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Low** | Haiku | Mechanical, verifiable, high volume |
| **Mid** | Sonnet | Follows a spec, produces structure |
| **Top** | Opus | Taste, synthesis, judgment, anything human-facing |

| Step | Tier | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **0 Bootstrap** | Low | Capability checks with right answers |
| **1 Intake** | **Top** | Reading a human, and the goal underneath the stated goal |
| **1 Competitor teardown** (`market-analyst`) | Mid | Charting against a fixed rubric |
| **1 Reading the chart** | **Top** | Which empty position is defensible |
| **1 VOC mining** (`voice-miner`) | Low–Mid | Collection is mechanical; extracting the recurring phrase is mid |
| **1 Crawl + redirect map** (`evidence-auditor`) | Low | URLs in, URLs out. A right answer exists |
| **1 Claim substantiation** (`evidence-auditor`) | Mid | Judgment about what a source supports (`§6`) |
| **1 Positioning + message hierarchy** | **Top** | The strategy is here. Every later loop consumes it |
| **Gate A** | **Top** | Presenting options to a human and hearing the reaction |
| **2a Concepts** | **Top** | The collision, the opening move, the thing nobody expects (`§2–3`) |
| **2a Design images** (`section-designer`) | Mid | Executes an approved direction |
| **2b Technique assignment** | **Top** | Which technique serves this buyer, and the commercial cut test |
| **2b Prototypes** (`technique-prototyper`) | Mid | Build it, measure it, report honestly |
| **Gates B1 / B2** | **Top** | Judgment on rendered work |
| **3 The headline** | **Top** | The highest-leverage sentence on the site |
| **3 Page copy** (`page-writer`) | Mid | Drafting to an approved hierarchy |
| **3 Voice and slop pass** | **Top** | Sounding like the customer rather than like a model (`§20`) |
| **3 Claims check** | Mid | Cross-referencing copy against `EVIDENCE.md` |
| **4 Page builds** (`page-builder`) | Mid | Coding to an approved image with the design settled |
| **4 Vendoring, budget, meta** | Low | Mechanical with a pass condition |
| **5 Forms, CRM, events** | Mid | Wiring to a spec, with a testable outcome |
| **5 OG image and share** | Mid | Design work inside a settled system |
| **5 Consent configuration** | Mid | Rule-following with legal consequences (`§16`) |
| **6 Deploy commands** | Low | Adapter commands with right answers |
| **6 Gate C and go/no-go** | **Top** | Irreversible, and the gate that never skips |
| **7 Checklist** (`site-verifier`) | Low | axe, Lighthouse, links, redirects. Pass or fail |
| **7 Funnel proof** (`funnel-verifier`) | Mid | Multi-step, stateful, and it has to notice a wrong result |

Which tier of model runs which step, and who decides.

and the split is not where most people put it.

A step where a mistake is caught by the next command is cheap to get wrong. A step
whose output every later loop consumes is expensive to get wrong, and no amount of
downstream quality repairs it.

   sitemap, building a redirect map, vendoring a library, running axe, checking that
   an event fired — all have right answers.

   approved design image, charting competitors against a fixed rubric, drafting a

# Skipping

Everything in this pipeline is optional except six things. The client decides how much
of it to run. Your job is to state the cost once, honor the answer, and record it —
not to argue, and not to quietly lower the bar without saying so.

## The six that never skip

| Rule | Why it can't be traded |
|---|---|
| `§6` Every claim traces to evidence | A number on a company site is an advertising claim, and the client carries it after you leave |
| `§13` Don't break what ranks | An unredirected redesign destroys traffic that took years to earn, invisibly, for weeks |
| `§16` Consent before tracking | Firing a tag before consent is the violation, and it is the client's liability |
| `§17` Accessibility basics | Legal exposure in most markets, and a form nobody can complete with a keyboard is a lead lost silently |
| `§18` The conversion path works end to end | A form that posts to nowhere looks fine and loses every lead, for months |
| `§23` Deploy is reversible, and you push as them | Without a snapshot a bad deploy destroys what was there, and credentials belong to the client |

Plus **Gate C**: nothing becomes publicly visible on a company's domain before the
person accountable has seen it.

If asked to skip one of these, say once that it is not available, offer the nearest
thing that is, and continue with everything else. Two of them come up regularly:

- *"We don't need the redirect stuff, the old site was rubbish."* The old site's
  rankings are not rubbish. The map takes an hour and it is the difference between a
  redesign and a traffic loss the client will blame the redesign for.
- *"Just put the cookie banner on later."* Later is after the tags are live, which is
  after the violation.

## How a skip works

1. The client says skip. One sentence from you: what it would have caught.
2. They confirm. **That's the end of it** — never raise it again, never hedge the rest
   of the run with it.
3. Append to `runs/<slug>/SKIPS.md`: the step, their reason if given, the cost.
4. The confidence grade in `REPORT.md` reflects it.

Never skip a step on your own initiative to save time. Skipping is the client's call.

## The skip ledger

Each loop file repeats its own row. This is the whole map.

| Step | Skipping it costs you |
|---|---|
| **1 Intake** | The goal, in numbers, and the constraint underneath the stated brief. Without it the run cannot be evaluated and Gate A becomes taste. Highest-cost skip in the pipeline. |
| **1 Stakeholder interviews** | Sales and support know the objections that stop deals. Skipping means the site answers the objections the founder remembers. |
| **1 VOC mining** | The customer's words (`§5`). Copy reverts to the company's own vocabulary, which is the most common reason a well-designed site converts badly. |
| **1 Competitor teardown** | The fence and the empty position. You design blind to what the buyer is comparing against, and `§3` becomes guesswork. |
| **1 Brand audit** | Knowing what is load-bearing. Design drifts into an accidental rebrand nobody signed off. |
| **1 Baseline metrics** | Loop 8 has nothing to compare against. Every claim about the redesign becomes an opinion, including the client's. Costs ten minutes. |
| **1 Positioning synthesis** | The message hierarchy and the translation table. Design and copy stop being derivable and become taste. |
| **Architecture decision** | Defaults to the smallest shape. Cheap to be wrong about while nothing is built. Discovering at Loop 4 that the committee needs a security page and three case-study URLs means rebuilding the shell, the nav, and the share layer. |
| **2a Design images** | Seeing it before it is built. You iterate in code instead: slower, and biased toward whatever got built first. |
| **Gate B1** | The concept choice. You pick; they see it at Gate C, which is late to discover a disagreement. |
| **2b Prototypes** | Proof the technique works before the design depends on it. Late failures are expensive. |
| **Gate B2** | Motion review, the performance budget, and the third-party tag list — which means tags get added later with no owner. |
| **3 Copy** | Real words. Design gets built around placeholder lengths and breaks when actual text arrives. On a marketing site copy *is* the product. |
| **3 Objection mapping** | Answers land in a bottom FAQ, where objections go to be ignored. |
| **3 Claims check** | `§6` is hard; this is how it is enforced. Not skippable in substance, only in thoroughness. |
| **4 Build quality passes** | Cross-browser and responsive correctness caught before deploy rather than after. |
| **5 Analytics and events** | Loop 8, and any ability to say whether the run worked. See [`MEASURE.md`](./MEASURE.md). |
| **5 CRM wiring** | Leads arrive in an inbox someone has to remember to check. Acceptable if that person is real and named. |
| **5 Share layer** | The unfurl. The link gets pasted into Slack by the champion and shows a gray box — the first impression the buying committee gets, before the site loads. Cheapest step in the pipeline to keep. |
| **5 Structured data** | Rich results, and some free credibility in the SERP. |
| **6 Deploy** | Nothing goes live. Output is a build folder and instructions. A legitimate end state — agency handoff mode. |
| **7 Verify** | Confirmation it renders and converts on real devices. Skipping means the first person to find the broken form is a customer. |
| **7 Redirect verification** | The `§13` work, unconfirmed. A redirect map that was written but never tested is not a redirect map. |
| **8 Measure** | The compounding half of this pipeline. The first version is a hypothesis; Loop 8 is where it starts paying. |
| **Handover** | They come back to you for every price change, or the change never happens. The second is more common, and it is how a site that launched well ends up with a 2023 price on it. |
| **Model tiering** | Matching the model to the work ([`MODELS.md`](./MODELS.md)). The quiet skip: on a low-tier session nothing fails a Loop 7 check and the copy converts worse. Note the session tier here so the grade means something. |
| **i18n / RTL** | Only skippable when there is one market and one script. Otherwise `§26` applies and it is not optional. |
| **Legal pages** | Only skippable when nothing is collected and no market requires an imprint. If there is a form, this is a legal requirement rather than a preference ([`COMPLIANCE.md`](./COMPLIANCE.md)). |

## Express mode

The pre-packaged skip set, for "we need this live before the conference":

- **Runs:** short intake (goal, ICP, offer, must-haves, do-nots), one competitor
  teardown, VOC from public reviews only, brand audit, redirect map, one concept,
  direct build, copy, capture layer, deploy, verify.
- **Skips:** stakeholder round, deep VOC, peer chart beyond one competitor, design
  images, prototypes, Gates B1 and B2, structured data, Loop 8 for now.
- **Keeps:** all six hard rules and Gate C. Non-negotiable, including on a deadline —
  the redirect map and the form test are the two things a rushed launch most needs.
- **Grade ceiling:** **B**.

Offer it when the client signals time pressure. Don't default to it.

## Landing-page mode

Not a skip set — a different shape. One page, one offer, one audience, usually behind
paid traffic.

Runs the same loops at smaller scale: intake and offer design matter *more* because
there is nowhere else for the argument to live; architecture is trivial; the SEO half
of Loop 5 shrinks to meta and speed; and Loop 8 matters more rather than less, because
a landing page exists to be iterated against a number.

Grade ceiling: **A**. It is a full run, just a small one.

## Confidence grade

Goes at the top of `REPORT.md`, with the reason.

| Grade | Means |
|---|---|
| **A** | Full pipeline. Claims substantiated, positioning derived from real market and customer evidence, design validated at both gates, funnel proven live, instrumented and measurable. |
| **B** | Core intact, some validation skipped. Strategy or design review thinner than ideal. Everything hard still held. |
| **C** | Substance skipped — no VOC, no competitor work, or no real copy pass. A good-looking site making the client's own claims in the client's own words. |
| **D** | Multiple substance skips, or shipped without measurement. Effectively a redesign whose effect nobody will ever know. Say exactly that. |

Report the grade honestly. A **D** stated clearly is more useful than an **A** claimed
falsely — the point of the grade is that the client knows what they have, and Loop 8
is the place it either gets defended or corrected.

# How to run it

## Claude Code

Install as a plugin, then:

```
/webcrab <company name or domain>
```

Or point at the skill directly: "read `skills/webcrab/SKILL.md` and run the pipeline
for \<client\>."

## Any other capable agent

Point it at this repo and say:

> Read `PRINCIPLES.md`, then `skills/webcrab/SKILL.md`. Execute the loops in `loops/`
> in order for \<client\>. Stop at every gate and wait for my decision.

There is no program to install. The pipeline is markdown; the agent is the runtime.

## Before you start, get these

The run goes much better if the client brings them. Ask on day zero:

| Thing | Why | If they can't |
|---|---|---|
| **The goal in numbers** | `§0`. Everything is accountable to it | Loop 1 derives one with them, and Loop 8 sets a baseline instead of beating one |
| **Analytics access** | The baseline, and where the leads currently come from | Record the gap; Loop 5 installs measurement from zero |
| **Search Console access** | The authoritative list of what ranks (`§13`) | Crawl instead, and accept that orphan pages will be missed |
| **Who can say yes** | One name (`§1`) | Gate A stalls in committee. Get the name |
| **Brand assets** | Logo files, type licenses, a brand book if one exists | Loop 1 audits what is on the current site and extends from there |
| **Customer material** | Reviews, support tickets, sales-call notes, churn reasons | VOC falls back to public review sites only, which is thinner |
| **Claims they want to make** | Every number, with where it came from (`§6`) | Anything unsourced gets cut or hedged, and they find out at Gate A rather than at launch |
| **Permissions** | Customer logo consents, testimonial approvals (`§25`) | Class instead of instance: "a national grocery chain" |

# Loop 0 — Bootstrap

**Goal:** confirm you can actually do the work before you promise any of it.

**Output:** a capability line in `runs/<slug>/REPORT.md`. Nothing else.

---

## The capabilities

| # | Capability | Native check | If missing |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Shell + git** | `git --version` | Stop. Nothing works without it |
| 2 | **Web fetch / search** | your own tools | Loop 1 competitor teardown and VOC mining are unavailable. Record the skip |
| 3 | **Headless browser** | `browse` skill, or Playwright | Loops 2b, 4, 7 lose screenshots and Loop 7 loses the funnel proof. **This is the one to fix** — `§18` needs a real browser |
| 4 | **Crawler** | `npx lychee`, or `wget --spider`, or the browser | Loop 1's redirect map is built from the sitemap alone, which misses orphan pages (`§13`) |
| 5 | **Image generation** | `imagegen-frontend-web` or equivalent | Loop 2a runs as written concepts instead of images; Gate B1 gets worse |
| 6 | **Image sampling** | `python3 -c "import PIL"` | `pip install Pillow`, or ImageMagick, or the brand palette gets guessed (`§12`) |
| 7 | **Prose skills** | `stop-slop`, `copywriting`, `ogilvy` | Install via `find-skills`. Loop 3 degrades without them |
| 8 | **Audit tooling** | `npx @axe-core/cli`, `npx lighthouse` | Loop 7 checks become manual. `§17` still applies |
| 9 | **GitHub API** | `gh auth status` | Only needed if the client's repo or Pages is the target |
| 10 | **Deploy CLI** | depends on target — see below | Loop 6 becomes handoff mode |

Check them, report what you have in one line, and move on. Do not spend a long time
here.

## Client-side access — ask, don't check

Four things you cannot verify yourself and should ask for now, so they exist by the
time they are needed. They are the most common reason a run stalls in the middle.

| Access | Needed by | Ask for |
|---|---|---|
| Analytics | Loop 1 baseline, Loop 5, Loop 8 | Read access on their property, on their account |
| Search Console | Loop 1 redirect map, Loop 7, Loop 8 | Verified property access — the authoritative ranking list |
| CRM / lead destination | Loop 5, Loop 7 (`§18`) | Where leads go, who reads them, and a way to confirm arrival |
| DNS and host | Loop 6 | Whose account, who can change records, current TTL |

## The deploy CLI

Cannot be checked until the target is known, which happens in Loop 1. Re-run this row
after Gate A.

| Target | Check |
|---|---|
| GitHub Pages | `gh auth status` |
| Netlify | `netlify --version` |
| Vercel | `vercel --version` |
| Cloudflare Pages | `wrangler --version` |
| VPS (nginx or Docker) | `ssh <host> 'echo ok'`, then `docker --version` on the host if relevant |
| cPanel | `lftp --version`, or `curl --version` with FTPS |
| S3 + CloudFront | `aws sts get-caller-identity` |
| Handoff | nothing |

A missing CLI is not a blocker. Say which one, offer to install it, and continue — the
target only has to work by Loop 6.

## Set up the run

```bash
mkdir -p runs/<slug>/{shots,prototypes,inbox,design,baseline}
cp runs/_template/*.md runs/<slug>/
```

`<slug>` is the client's domain or name, lowercased and hyphenated. `inbox/` is where
they drop material for Loop 1 — brand book, sales deck, customer quotes, support
exports, the claims they want to make. Tell them it exists now, so the material is
there by the time you need it.

`baseline/` is where Loop 1's analytics exports and screenshots go. It is small,
boring, and the only reason Loop 8 can say anything honest.

## Existing site or not

One question, asked here rather than in Loop 1, because the answer changes what Loop 1
has to do first.

| Answer | Loop 1 must also |
|---|---|
| Replacing a site on the same domain | Crawl it, export the ranking URLs, build the redirect map (`§13`, hard). Capture the baseline before anything changes |
| New domain, nothing to replace | One sentence: "nothing to preserve." Move on |
| New site, old one stays somewhere | Decide what happens to the old URLs. "Both live" is usually two sites competing for the same terms |

## What not to do here

Do not research the client. Do not propose a design. Do not ask the intake questions —
those belong to Loop 1 and they work better opening the conversation than following a
capability audit.

## Skip cost

Skipping bootstrap costs you a failure in Loop 6 or 7 instead of a two-minute check in
Loop 0, plus the client-access requests arriving three loops late. It is the cheapest
loop to run and the most annoying one to have skipped.
