# Loop 1 — Market & Message

**Goal:** end this loop knowing what the site has to achieve in numbers, who it is
for, what they compare it against, what they will object to, what is actually true,
and what must not break. Every decision downstream is derived from this loop. Nothing
after it guesses.

**Output:** `BRIEF.md` (the one source), `EVIDENCE.md` (every claim, sourced),
`redirects.csv` (`§13`), and `baseline/` (the numbers before anything changed).

```text
1a INTAKE ─► 1b STAKEHOLDERS ─► 1c MARKET ─► 1d EVIDENCE ─► 1e SYNTHESIS ─► Gate A
   goal +       sales, support     competitors,  claims,       BRIEF.md
   vision       the objections     VOC, search   crawl,        + message hierarchy
                they actually      demand        redirects,    + translation table
                hear                             baseline
```

The order is deliberate. Intake first because the goal frames everything and unprimed
answers are better answers. Stakeholders second because sales and support know the
objections the founder has stopped hearing. Market third. Evidence last, because by
then you know which claims matter enough to substantiate.

Much of 1c and 1d is autonomous and runs in parallel with 1a and 1b — dispatch
`market-analyst`, `voice-miner`, and `evidence-auditor` early and let them work while
you talk.

---

## 1a — Intake (`§0`)

**The conductor runs this. Never delegate it** — a subagent cannot talk to the human.

This is the most expensive step in the pipeline to get wrong, and the instinct to run
discovery cheap is exactly backwards ([`MODELS.md`](../MODELS.md)). Everything
downstream consumes `BRIEF.md`. If the session is on a lower tier, say so once here
and continue either way.

Ask **one question at a time**. Open-ended. Do not offer multiple choice — the answer
has to be theirs. Follow the thread. React to what they actually said before moving on.

### The goal

> What is the one action you want someone to take on this site?
>
> How many of those do you get a month right now, and out of how many visitors?
>
> What number would make this project obviously worth doing?
>
> What is one of those worth to you, and what proportion close?
>
> What happens if this doesn't work — what is the actual consequence, and by when?
>
> Who inside your company has to be happy with this, and who can say yes on their own?

That last question is `§1`. Get one name, written down, before Gate A. Everyone
else's feedback is input.

### The vision

> What should someone feel in the first three seconds, before they have read a word?
>
> Name a site — in any industry — that made you jealous. What specifically did it do?
>
> If this company were a physical place, what is it: a workshop, a bank, a lab, a
> market stall, a members' club?
>
> Should it feel like it was made in 1972, 2004, or 2041?
>
> What is the one thing on your current site you would keep, and the one you would
> burn?

### The business

> Describe your best customer. Not the biggest — the one you wish you had ten more of.
>
> What just happened in their week that made them go looking? Be specific about the
> week.
>
> What do they do today instead of buying from you?
>
> Why do people say no? Give me the last three.
>
> What do you turn down, and what does turning it down cost you?
>
> Who is the competitor you lose to most, and what do they get wrong?
>
> What do you know about this market that your competitors have not worked out yet?
>
> If a customer had to explain you to their boss in one sentence, what would you want
> them to say?

### The practical set

> What is the offer today — what does someone actually get when they say yes, and how
> long do they wait? (Walk the friction ladder in [`CONVERSION.md`](../CONVERSION.md))
>
> Every number you want on the site — where did each one come from, and when was it
> last true? (`§6`)
>
> Which customer logos can we use, and do you have that in writing? (`§25`)
>
> What cannot be shown at all: clients under NDA, unlaunched products, numbers that
> were never public?
>
> Must-haves — anything you explicitly want in it.
>
> Do-nots — colors, words, styles, a competitor's look, a phrase legal hates.
>
> Which markets and sectors do you sell into? (Drives [`COMPLIANCE.md`](../COMPLIANCE.md))
>
> Where does it deploy, and whose account is it on?
>
> After launch, who changes the pricing page, and what did they change on the current
> site in the last six months? (`ARCHITECTURE.md` — take the second answer as the real
> one)

Invite references throughout: sites, brands, a physical space, a magazine, a store.
Feel is an input.

**Record verbatim.** Their actual sentences become the company register in
`POSITIONING.md §11`. Paraphrase destroys the only voice sample there is.

If they don't know an answer, offer directions and let them react. Do not stall.

## 1b — The stakeholder round

The founder's answers are one view, and usually the oldest one. Twenty minutes each
with the people who talk to customers is the cheapest research in this pipeline.

| Who | Ask |
|---|---|
| **Sales** | What is the first question on every call? What objection kills deals? Which page do you send, and what do you have to explain because the site doesn't? What do you wish you could stop repeating? |
| **Support** | What do customers get wrong about what this does? What do they say when they are annoyed? What do the good ones say when they get it? |
| **Customer success / churn** | Why do people leave, and what did they expect that they did not get? A site that oversells produces churn, and the client will not connect the two |
| **The person who answers the inbox** | What actually arrives through the form? Is any of it useful? |
| **Product / engineering** | What is genuinely hard about this that competitors cannot copy? What are we claiming that is not quite true yet? |

The last question in that final row protects `§6` and it is easier to get from an
engineer than from a founder.

Two conflicts will surface: sales wanting the site to qualify harder and marketing
wanting more leads, and the founder's description not matching what support hears.
Both go to Gate A as findings, not as things you resolved on your own.

## 1c — Market

Two autonomous jobs, dispatched in parallel.

### Competitor teardown (`market-analyst`)

3–6 competitors — the ones that actually appear when the ICP searches, not the ones
on the board slide. Chart each per `POSITIONING.md §5`: hero line verbatim, claimed
differentiator, lead proof, pricing visibility, offer and its friction, style family,
palette, page shape.

Then read the chart, which is the top-tier half: where they cluster, what position is
empty, and what the buyer's comparison looks like when they open three tabs.

### Voice of the customer (`voice-miner`)

`§5`, and the highest-leverage research in the loop.

Sources, in rough order of value: the client's own support tickets and sales-call
notes, review platforms for the client and every competitor, the relevant subreddit or
forum, competitor churn complaints, and Search Console's existing query data.

What comes back: 10–20 recurring phrases with fingerprints on them, the top objections
ranked by frequency, the words customers use for the *problem* (which is almost never
the words the client uses for the *product*), and the outcomes they say they got.

**Competitor reviews are the richest source available.** The one-star reviews of the
market leader are a list of the objections this client can answer, written by the
people who have them.

### Search demand ([`SEO.md`](../SEO.md))

What the ICP types, sorted by intent. It decides which pages exist, so it belongs here
rather than in Loop 5.

## 1d — Evidence, the crawl, and the baseline

`evidence-auditor` runs all three.

### Substantiate the claims (`§6`, hard)

Every number, superlative, comparison, and certification the client wants on the site,
with its source and its date. Rank each on the proof ladder (`POSITIONING.md §10`).
Anything unsourced comes back as a question, not as a cut you made silently.

Hunt for a rank-1 proof point. Most clients have one and do not know it — a support
metric, a churn number, a customer who will say a sentence on the record, a public
benchmark. Finding one is often the highest-value thing this loop does.

### Crawl the old site and build the redirect map (`§13`, hard)

Per [`SEO.md`](../SEO.md) Part 1: sitemap, crawl, Search Console's 12-month page list,
analytics landing pages, backlinks, paid landing pages. Then `redirects.csv`, one row
per existing URL, 301s, no chains, nearest relevant target.

This is mechanical and it is not optional when a site already exists.

### Capture the baseline ([`MEASURE.md`](../MEASURE.md))

Export and screenshot into `runs/<slug>/baseline/`: sessions, conversions, conversion
rate, traffic by source, top 20 landing pages, top 20 queries, Core Web Vitals — all
for the last 12 months.

Ten minutes, and it is the only reason Loop 8 can say anything honest. Analytics
properties get reconfigured mid-project and the comparison disappears with them.

### Brand audit (`§12`)

Per `POSITIONING.md §12`. Sample the palette from what exists, check type licensing,
find what fails contrast, and separate load-bearing from accidental. Write the
extension you propose. **A rebrand is a Gate A decision, never drift.**

## 1e — Synthesis

Now write the strategy, following [`POSITIONING.md`](../POSITIONING.md) exactly:

1. **The goal in numbers** — with the baseline beside it
2. **ICP** — role, company shape, buying committee, trigger, alternatives
3. **Jobs to be done** — three, ranked, in the customer's words
4. **Category** — compete, subdivide, or create, with the cost named
5. **Competitive reading** — cluster, empty position, the comparison they will run
6. **Positioning statement** — the forced sentence, passing the competitor test and
   the proof test
7. **Anti-positioning** — until one entry hurts
8. **Message hierarchy** — five levels, and every page will map to it
9. **Objection ladder** — ranked from VOC, each with where it is felt
10. **Proof ladder** — every claim ranked, weak ones demoted or cut
11. **Voice** — customer lexicon and company register, kept separate
12. **Brand** — load-bearing, accidental, broken, and the proposed extension
13. **Site shape and page list** — from [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](../ARCHITECTURE.md)
14. **The translation table** — every row filled

This is top-tier work and the conductor does it rather than a worker.

## Write the outputs

**`EVIDENCE.md`** — every claim, its source, its date, its rank, and where it will
appear. Contradictions between sources. What was cut. The permissions status of every
logo and testimonial (`§25`).

**`BRIEF.md`** — the intake record verbatim, the stakeholder findings, the evidence
summary, the competitive chart and its reading, the VOC extract, and all fourteen
synthesis sections.

**`redirects.csv`** and **`baseline/`** — as above.

> ## Gate A — human decision
>
> The named decision-maker from `§1` decides. Present:
>
> - The goal in numbers, and the baseline it is measured against
> - ICP, the trigger, and the buying committee
> - Positioning statement and anti-positioning — expect resistance to the entries that
>   hurt, and hold them
> - The competitive gap you found, and whether to occupy it
> - The offer and its rung on the friction ladder (`CONVERSION.md §1`) — bring the
>   ladder, not one answer
> - The top three objections and where each gets answered
> - Every claim that failed substantiation, and what happens to it (`§6`)
> - The page list, the site shape, and who edits it afterward
> - The redirect map, and any ranking page whose message the redesign would change
> - The deploy target and whose accounts everything sits on
>
> Bring 2–3 readings where the strategy is genuinely ambiguous (`§4`), not one answer.
> They approve, adjust, or send you back. Do not proceed without a decision.
>
> The site shape and the page list are settled here and not revisited. Discovering at
> Loop 4 that the buying committee needs a security page means rebuilding the shell,
> the nav, and the share layer.

## Skip costs

| Skipping | Costs |
|---|---|
| 1a Intake | The goal in numbers and the constraint underneath the brief. Gate A becomes taste and Loop 8 has nothing to grade. Highest-cost skip in the pipeline |
| 1b Stakeholders | The objections that actually stop deals. You answer the ones the founder remembers |
| 1c Competitors | The fence and the empty position. `§3` becomes guesswork |
| 1c VOC | The customer's words (`§5`). Copy reverts to company vocabulary — the most common reason a well-designed site converts badly |
| 1d Evidence | `§6` is hard. Not skippable in substance, only in thoroughness — and thoroughness is what keeps a stale number off the homepage |
| 1d Crawl / redirects | `§13` is hard. Not available |
| 1d Baseline | Loop 8 becomes an opinion. Ten minutes |
| 1d Brand audit | What is load-bearing. Design drifts into an unsigned rebrand |
| 1e Synthesis | The message hierarchy and translation table. Design and copy stop being derivable |

**Output:** `BRIEF.md` (the one source), `EVIDENCE.md` (every claim, sourced),
`redirects.csv` (`§13`), and `baseline/` (the numbers before anything changed).

```text
1a INTAKE ─► 1b STAKEHOLDERS ─► 1c MARKET ─► 1d EVIDENCE ─► 1e SYNTHESIS ─► Gate A
   goal +       sales, support     competitors,  claims,       BRIEF.md
   vision       the objections     VOC, search   crawl,        + message hierarchy
                they actually      demand        redirects,    + translation table
                hear                             baseline
```

The order is deliberate. Intake first because the goal frames everything and unprimed
answers are better answers. Stakeholders second because sales and support know the
objections the founder has stopped hearing. Market third. Evidence last, because by
then you know which claims matter enough to substantiate.

Much of 1c and 1d is autonomous and runs in parallel with 1a and 1b — dispatch
`market-analyst`, `voice-miner`, and `evidence-auditor` early and let them work while
you talk.

---

## 1a — Intake (`§0`)

**The conductor runs this. Never delegate it** — a subagent cannot talk to the human.

This is the most expensive step in the pipeline to get wrong, and the instinct to run
discovery cheap is exactly backwards ([`MODELS.md`](../MODELS.md)). Everything
downstream consumes `BRIEF.md`. If the session is on a lower tier, say so once here
and continue either way.

Ask **one question at a time**. Open-ended. Do not offer multiple choice — the answer
has to be theirs. Follow the thread. React to what they actually said before moving on.

### The goal

> What is the one action you want someone to take on this site?
>
> How many of those do you get a month right now, and out of how many visitors?
>
> What number would make this project obviously worth doing?
>
> What is one of those worth to you, and what proportion close?
>
> What happens if this doesn't work — what is the actual consequence, and by when?
>
> Who inside your company has to be happy with this, and who can say yes on their own?

That last question is `§1`. Get one name, written down, before Gate A. Everyone
else's feedback is input.

### The vision

> What should someone feel in the first three seconds, before they have read a word?
>
> Name a site — in any industry — that made you jealous. What specifically did it do?
>
> If this company were a physical place, what is it: a workshop, a bank, a lab, a
> market stall, a members' club?
>
> Should it feel like it was made in 1972, 2004, or 2041?
>
> What is the one thing on your current site you would keep, and the one you would
> burn?

### The business

> Describe your best customer. Not the biggest — the one you wish you had ten more of.
>
> What just happened in their week that made them go looking? Be specific about the
> week.
>
> What do they do today instead of buying from you?
>
> Why do people say no? Give me the last three.
>
> What do you turn down, and what does turning it down cost you?
>
> Who is the competitor you lose to most, and what do they get wrong?
>
> What do you know about this market that your competitors have not worked out yet?
>
> If a customer had to explain you to their boss in one sentence, what would you want
> them to say?

### The practical set

> What is the offer today — what does someone actually get when they say yes, and how
> long do they wait? (Walk the friction ladder in [`CONVERSION.md`](../CONVERSION.md))
>
> Every number you want on the site — where did each one come from, and when was it
> last true? (`§6`)
>
> Which customer logos can we use, and do you have that in writing? (`§25`)
>
> What cannot be shown at all: clients under NDA, unlaunched products, numbers that
> were never public?
>
> Must-haves — anything you explicitly want in it.
>
> Do-nots — colors, words, styles, a competitor's look, a phrase legal hates.
>
> Which markets and sectors do you sell into? (Drives [`COMPLIANCE.md`](../COMPLIANCE.md))
>
> Where does it deploy, and whose account is it on?
>
> After launch, who changes the pricing page, and what did they change on the current
> site in the last six months? (`ARCHITECTURE.md` — take the second answer as the real
> one)

Invite references throughout: sites, brands, a physical space, a magazine, a store.
Feel is an input.

**Record verbatim.** Their actual sentences become the company register in
`POSITIONING.md §11`. Paraphrase destroys the only voice sample there is.

If they don't know an answer, offer directions and let them react. Do not stall.

## 1b — The stakeholder round

The founder's answers are one view, and usually the oldest one. Twenty minutes each
with the people who talk to customers is the cheapest research in this pipeline.

| Who | Ask |
|---|---|
| **Sales** | What is the first question on every call? What objection kills deals? Which page do you send, and what do you have to explain because the site doesn't? What do you wish you could stop repeating? |
| **Support** | What do customers get wrong about what this does? What do they say when they are annoyed? What do the good ones say when they get it? |
| **Customer success / churn** | Why do people leave, and what did they expect that they did not get? A site that oversells produces churn, and the client will not connect the two |
| **The person who answers the inbox** | What actually arrives through the form? Is any of it useful? |
| **Product / engineering** | What is genuinely hard about this that competitors cannot copy? What are we claiming that is not quite true yet? |

The last question in that final row protects `§6` and it is easier to get from an
engineer than from a founder.

Two conflicts will surface: sales wanting the site to qualify harder and marketing
wanting more leads, and the founder's description not matching what support hears.
Both go to Gate A as findings, not as things you resolved on your own.

## 1c — Market

Two autonomous jobs, dispatched in parallel.

### Competitor teardown (`market-analyst`)

3–6 competitors — the ones that actually appear when the ICP searches, not the ones
on the board slide. Chart each per `POSITIONING.md §5`: hero line verbatim, claimed
differentiator, lead proof, pricing visibility, offer and its friction, style family,
palette, page shape.

Then read the chart, which is the top-tier half: where they cluster, what position is
empty, and what the buyer's comparison looks like when they open three tabs.

### Voice of the customer (`voice-miner`)

`§5`, and the highest-leverage research in the loop.

Sources, in rough order of value: the client's own support tickets and sales-call
notes, review platforms for the client and every competitor, the relevant subreddit or
forum, competitor churn complaints, and Search Console's existing query data.

What comes back: 10–20 recurring phrases with fingerprints on them, the top objections
ranked by frequency, the words customers use for the *problem* (which is almost never
the words the client uses for the *product*), and the outcomes they say they got.

**Competitor reviews are the richest source available.** The one-star reviews of the
market leader are a list of the objections this client can answer, written by the
people who have them.

### Search demand ([`SEO.md`](../SEO.md))

What the ICP types, sorted by intent. It decides which pages exist, so it belongs here
rather than in Loop 5.

## 1d — Evidence, the crawl, and the baseline

`evidence-auditor` runs all three.

### Substantiate the claims (`§6`, hard)

Every number, superlative, comparison, and certification the client wants on the site,
with its source and its date. Rank each on the proof ladder (`POSITIONING.md §10`).
Anything unsourced comes back as a question, not as a cut you made silently.

Hunt for a rank-1 proof point. Most clients have one and do not know it — a support
metric, a churn number, a customer who will say a sentence on the record, a public
benchmark. Finding one is often the highest-value thing this loop does.

### Crawl the old site and build the redirect map (`§13`, hard)

Per [`SEO.md`](../SEO.md) Part 1: sitemap, crawl, Search Console's 12-month page list,
analytics landing pages, backlinks, paid landing pages. Then `redirects.csv`, one row
per existing URL, 301s, no chains, nearest relevant target.

This is mechanical and it is not optional when a site already exists.

### Capture the baseline ([`MEASURE.md`](../MEASURE.md))

Export and screenshot into `runs/<slug>/baseline/`: sessions, conversions, conversion
rate, traffic by source, top 20 landing pages, top 20 queries, Core Web Vitals — all
for the last 12 months.

Ten minutes, and it is the only reason Loop 8 can say anything honest. Analytics
properties get reconfigured mid-project and the comparison disappears with them.

### Brand audit (`§12`)

Per `POSITIONING.md §12`. Sample the palette from what exists, check type licensing,
find what fails contrast, and separate load-bearing from accidental. Write the
extension you propose. **A rebrand is a Gate A decision, never drift.**

## 1e — Synthesis

Now write the strategy, following [`POSITIONING.md`](../POSITIONING.md) exactly:

1. **The goal in numbers** — with the baseline beside it
2. **ICP** — role, company shape, buying committee, trigger, alternatives
3. **Jobs to be done** — three, ranked, in the customer's words
4. **Category** — compete, subdivide, or create, with the cost named
5. **Competitive reading** — cluster, empty position, the comparison they will run
6. **Positioning statement** — the forced sentence, passing the competitor test and
   the proof test
7. **Anti-positioning** — until one entry hurts
8. **Message hierarchy** — five levels, and every page will map to it
9. **Objection ladder** — ranked from VOC, each with where it is felt
10. **Proof ladder** — every claim ranked, weak ones demoted or cut
11. **Voice** — customer lexicon and company register, kept separate
12. **Brand** — load-bearing, accidental, broken, and the proposed extension
13. **Site shape and page list** — from [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](../ARCHITECTURE.md)
14. **The translation table** — every row filled

This is top-tier work and the conductor does it rather than a worker.

## Write the outputs

**`EVIDENCE.md`** — every claim, its source, its date, its rank, and where it will
appear. Contradictions between sources. What was cut. The permissions status of every
logo and testimonial (`§25`).

**`BRIEF.md`** — the intake record verbatim, the stakeholder findings, the evidence
summary, the competitive chart and its reading, the VOC extract, and all fourteen
synthesis sections.

**`redirects.csv`** and **`baseline/`** — as above.

> ## Gate A — human decision
>
> The named decision-maker from `§1` decides. Present:
>
> - The goal in numbers, and the baseline it is measured against
> - ICP, the trigger, and the buying committee
> - Positioning statement and anti-positioning — expect resistance to the entries that
>   hurt, and hold them
> - The competitive gap you found, and whether to occupy it
> - The offer and its rung on the friction ladder (`CONVERSION.md §1`) — bring the
>   ladder, not one answer
> - The top three objections and where each gets answered
> - Every claim that failed substantiation, and what happens to it (`§6`)
> - The page list, the site shape, and who edits it afterward
> - The redirect map, and any ranking page whose message the redesign would change
> - The deploy target and whose accounts everything sits on
>
> Bring 2–3 readings where the strategy is genuinely ambiguous (`§4`), not one answer.
> They approve, adjust, or send you back. Do not proceed without a decision.
>
> The site shape and the page list are settled here and not revisited. Discovering at
> Loop 4 that the buying committee needs a security page means rebuilding the shell,
> the nav, and the share layer.

## Skip costs

| Skipping | Costs |
|---|---|
| 1a Intake | The goal in numbers and the constraint underneath the brief. Gate A becomes taste and Loop 8 has nothing to grade. Highest-cost skip in the pipeline |
| 1b Stakeholders | The objections that actually stop deals. You answer the ones the founder remembers |
| 1c Competitors | The fence and the empty position. `§3` becomes guesswork |
| 1c VOC | The customer's words (`§5`). Copy reverts to company vocabulary — the most common reason a well-designed site converts badly |
| 1d Evidence | `§6` is hard. Not skippable in substance, only in thoroughness — and thoroughness is what keeps a stale number off the homepage |
| 1d Crawl / redirects | `§13` is hard. Not available |
| 1d Baseline | Loop 8 becomes an opinion. Ten minutes |
| 1d Brand audit | What is load-bearing. Design drifts into an unsigned rebrand |
| 1e Synthesis | The message hierarchy and translation table. Design and copy stop being derivable |

# Loop 2 — Design

**Goal:** decide what it looks like and how it renders, and prove both before a single
line of the real site is written.

**Input:** `BRIEF.md`, specifically the translation table, the message hierarchy, and
the competitive chart.

**Output:** `DIRECTION.md`, one design image per section or template, one runnable
prototype per technique.

```text
2a DIRECTION ──────► Gate B1 ──────► 2b CRAFT ──────► Gate B2
   palette, type,     concept          technique per     motion, budget,
   2-3 concepts,      picked           section, motion    tag list locked
   image per section                   spec, prototypes
```

---

## 2a — Direction

### Read the translation table first

The style shortlist comes from strategy, not taste (`STYLES.md`):

- **The competitive cluster** is the fence. Whatever five of six competitors look
  like is what this site does not look like (`§3`)
- **The empty position** is the field
- **Anti-positioning** bans styles outright. Honor absolutely
- **The buyer's risk appetite** sets how strange you can be. A procurement committee
  and a founder buying a design sprint tolerate different amounts
- **Load-bearing brand elements** are constraints. Extensions were agreed at Gate A
- **The top objection** decides what the first screen has to do

### The page and section list is already fixed

Gate A settled which pages exist and what each is for. Loop 2 designs them; it does
not re-litigate them. If the design work reveals the page list is wrong, that goes
back to Gate A rather than being quietly changed — a page invented in Loop 2 has no
message-hierarchy slot and no copy plan.

Multi-page sites design **per template**, not per instance (`ARCHITECTURE.md`): home,
product, pricing, case study, blog post. One template covers every page that uses it.

### Palette

Sampled from reality (`§12`) — the existing logo, product, and real materials. Then
extended: an accent, a substrate, a neutral ramp, and a full state set including
error, success, warning, focus, and disabled, because this site has forms and the
forms need them.

Work in OKLCH so gradients have no gray dead zone. Check every text pair at 4.5:1 as
you build the ramp rather than after (`§17`), and check the brand accent as a button
background with white and with black text — a brand color that cannot hold a label is
a constraint to design around, not an opinion to argue with.

Art-direct **light and dark as two designs**, not one inverted. `STYLES.md` names
which styles collapse under naive inversion.

### Type

Two families at most, one if the style earns it. Variable where the design drives an
axis. Self-hosted, subset, `font-display: swap`. Confirm the web license covers the
client's use (`COMPLIANCE.md §3`) — an unlicensed font is a bill with their name on
it. Check the script renders for every market (`§26`).

### Concepts

Top-tier work, and the conductor does it rather than a worker
([`MODELS.md`](../MODELS.md)).

Generate **2–3 distinct concepts** (`§4`). Each states:

- The **collision or subversion** — this run's `§3` answer, in one sentence. Which
  parent carries structure, which carries surface
- The **opening move** — what happens in the first three seconds, and how the visitor
  learns what kind of thing this is (`POSITIONING.md §4`)
- How **proof is presented** — invent it. Not a logo bar and a testimonial slider by
  reflex
- How **the product is shown** (`§11`) — the single most consequential choice on a
  software marketing site
- How **pricing is displayed**, if there is a pricing page
- How **the ask** appears, where it repeats, and what it looks like on mobile
- How **navigation** works
- The **section order per template**, derived from the objection ladder rather than
  from convention

Run two checks on each concept before it goes to the gate:

1. **The category-reflex check.** If it is guessable from "site for a
   \<category\> company", or from category-plus-obvious-twist, throw it out
2. **The competitor overlay.** Put the concept beside the three competitor
   screenshots. If a visitor could not tell them apart in a squint test, it has not
   done its job

Note one concept you rejected and why, so the client sees the range.

### Design images

Dispatch `section-designer`, **one agent per section or template**. Each returns one
horizontal image.

Never compress multiple sections into one board. Eight sections means eight images. A
compressed board hides exactly the detail the client needs to judge — and on a
commercial site the detail that gets hidden is usually the CTA and the form.

Design at least one image with **real copy lengths** from the message hierarchy, not
lorem. A hero that only works with a six-word headline is a design that Loop 3 will
break.

> ## Gate B1 — human decision
>
> The named decision-maker decides. Present the rendered images per concept, the
> palette with its sampled sources and the contrast results, the type system, and the
> collision sentence for each. Show the competitor overlay — clients underestimate how
> much they look like their category until they see it side by side.
>
> They pick a concept, or pick pieces across concepts. Iterate here; it is far cheaper
> than iterating in code.

### When B1 rejects

How far back it goes depends on what was rejected. Diagnose before regenerating.

| What was rejected | Where it goes back to |
|---|---|
| **Execution** — wrong palette in the render, wrong crop, the image did not capture the concept | Regenerate the images with corrected direction. Same concept, same section list, same collision |
| **Concept** — the collision does not land, the opening move is wrong, proof is presented wrong | Back to 2a concept generation. New concepts, not a patch on the rejected one |
| **Strategy** — their reaction reveals the ICP, positioning, or objection ranking was misread | Back to Gate A. Fix `BRIEF.md` first. Designing on a misread brief produces another rejection |
| **Committee** — two stakeholders want opposite things | Not a design problem. Take it to the named decision-maker (`§1`) rather than averaging it into something neither wanted |

The last two rows are the ones that get missed. When the client says the images look
fine and still sounds unhappy, the brief is the suspect. When the feedback contradicts
itself, the process is.

**Three rejections at the same gate means the brief is wrong, not the execution.**
Stop iterating, re-open Loop 1e, and come back through Gate A.

## 2b — Craft

### Assign techniques

For each section, assign a technique from [`CRAFT.md`](../CRAFT.md) that serves the
approved style. Style decides what is on the table; the technique executes it.

Every assignment passes the commercial test in `CRAFT.md`:

1. What does this make the visitor **understand**?
2. Which **objection** does it answer or which **proof** does it carry?
3. What does it cost in **bytes and main-thread time**?

No answer to the first two means cut it. Impressive and irrelevant is not neutral on a
company site — it is scroll depth the converting section needed (`§7`).

**Spend the technique budget where the money is.** The hero, the product
demonstration, and the moment just before the ask. A beautifully animated
about-page timeline is budget taken from the pricing table.

### Prototype before you design around it

Dispatch `technique-prototyper`, **one agent per technique**. Each one researches
freely, builds a standalone runnable HTML proof, screenshots it, measures frame rate
under load on throttled hardware, records the byte cost, and builds all three states
(full, designed reduced-motion, fallback).

Prototypes live in `runs/<slug>/prototypes/`. A technique that fails here is cut now,
cheaply. The same failure in Loop 4 costs a rebuild.

### Motion spec

Write it down: easing curves, durations, stagger, scroll mapping, what triggers what.
Motion character comes from the positioning — an institutional brand moves slowly and
inevitably; a challenger moves abruptly. Undocumented motion gets rebuilt three times.

Two rules specific to commercial sites: **nothing animates in above the fold** (it is
already visible; animating it makes it briefly not), and **motion never gates
information** (a skimmer who cannot skim leaves).

### The third-party tag list (`§15`)

New at this gate, and it belongs here rather than in Loop 5, because tags are a
performance decision as much as a marketing one.

List every third party the client wants: analytics, chat, heatmap, ad pixels, review
widget, embedded booking, consent platform, tag manager. For each: the named owner,
the job it does, the data it sees, the byte cost, and when it loads relative to
consent and first paint.

Bring the list to the gate with a recommendation on what to cut. Marketing teams add
tags by default and nobody ever removes one; this is the only moment in the project
where the whole list is visible at once.

### The performance budget

Declare it, per `§19`:

- **Shell** — HTML, CSS, fonts, critical JS. Under 100KB. Paints something real alone.
  LCP under 2.0s on a throttled mid-range Android, targeting 1.5s
- **Heavy layer** — shaders, 3D, video, physics. Lazy-loaded after first paint, gated
  on intersection, never in the LCP path. State the number
- **Third-party** — the total from the tag list, with its own number

A technique that cannot be deferred has to justify its bytes at this gate, in front of
the client, against the conversion goal.

### Write `DIRECTION.md`

Concept and why it won. The collision, and which parent is structural. Palette with
hexes, sampled sources, and contrast results. Type system and licensing. Per-template
technique assignment. Motion spec. All three budget tiers. The tag list with owners.
**What was invented** — the thing that exists in this run and no other (`§3`).
Prototype results including the failures.

> ## Gate B2 — human decision
>
> Show the prototype screenshots, the motion spec, the three-tier budget, and the tag
> list. They approve the technique set or cut what does not earn its place, and they
> approve or cut each tag with its owner named.
>
> This is the last stop before real code.

### When B2 rejects

Cut the technique, or swap it for another from `CRAFT.md`, then re-prototype. A
rejected prototype never gets argued into acceptance, tuned during the build, or
carried forward on the theory that it comes together in integration.

The replacement faces the same three-question test. Cutting with nothing in its place
is a valid outcome — the section ships in its base state and the budget improves.

### A rejection is information about the brief

Record what the rejection **revealed** in `DIRECTION.md`, alongside the new direction:
what they reacted against, and what that says about the ICP, the buyer's risk
appetite, or the positioning that `BRIEF.md` failed to capture. Recording only the
correction throws away the more valuable half.

## Skip costs

| Skipping | Costs |
|---|---|
| 2a design images | Seeing it before it is built. You iterate in code instead: slower, and biased toward whatever got built first |
| Gate B1 | The concept choice. You pick; they see it at Gate C, which is a late place to discover a disagreement |
| 2b prototypes | Proof the technique works before the design depends on it. Late failures are expensive |
| 2b tag list | The only moment the whole third-party list is visible at once. Tags get added later with no owner and no budget |
| Gate B2 | Motion review, and the performance budget goes undeclared |

| **Execution** — wrong palette in the render, wrong crop, the image did not capture the concept | Regenerate the images with corrected direction. Same concept, same section list, same collision |
| **Concept** — the collision does not land, the opening move is wrong, proof is presented wrong | Back to 2a concept generation. New concepts, not a patch on the rejected one |
| **Strategy** — their reaction reveals the ICP, positioning, or objection ranking was misread | Back to Gate A. Fix `BRIEF.md` first. Designing on a misread brief produces another rejection |
| **Committee** — two stakeholders want opposite things | Not a design problem. Take it to the named decision-maker (`§1`) rather than averaging it into something neither wanted |

The last two rows are the ones that get missed. When the client says the images look
fine and still sounds unhappy, the brief is the suspect. When the feedback contradicts
itself, the process is.

**Three rejections at the same gate means the brief is wrong, not the execution.**
Stop iterating, re-open Loop 1e, and come back through Gate A.

## 2b — Craft

### Assign techniques

For each section, assign a technique from [`CRAFT.md`](../CRAFT.md) that serves the
approved style. Style decides what is on the table; the technique executes it.

Every assignment passes the commercial test in `CRAFT.md`:

1. What does this make the visitor **understand**?
2. Which **objection** does it answer or which **proof** does it carry?
3. What does it cost in **bytes and main-thread time**?

No answer to the first two means cut it. Impressive and irrelevant is not neutral on a
company site — it is scroll depth the converting section needed (`§7`).

**Spend the technique budget where the money is.** The hero, the product
demonstration, and the moment just before the ask. A beautifully animated
about-page timeline is budget taken from the pricing table.

### Prototype before you design around it

Dispatch `technique-prototyper`, **one agent per technique**. Each one researches
freely, builds a standalone runnable HTML proof, screenshots it, measures frame rate
under load on throttled hardware, records the byte cost, and builds all three states
(full, designed reduced-motion, fallback).

Prototypes live in `runs/<slug>/prototypes/`. A technique that fails here is cut now,
cheaply. The same failure in Loop 4 costs a rebuild.

### Motion spec

Write it down: easing curves, durations, stagger, scroll mapping, what triggers what.
Motion character comes from the positioning — an institutional brand moves slowly and
inevitably; a challenger moves abruptly. Undocumented motion gets rebuilt three times.

Two rules specific to commercial sites: **nothing animates in above the fold** (it is
already visible; animating it makes it briefly not), and **motion never gates
information** (a skimmer who cannot skim leaves).

### The third-party tag list (`§15`)

New at this gate, and it belongs here rather than in Loop 5, because tags are a
performance decision as much as a marketing one.

List every third party the client wants: analytics, chat, heatmap, ad pixels, review
widget, embedded booking, consent platform, tag manager. For each: the named owner,
the job it does, the data it sees, the byte cost, and when it loads relative to
consent and first paint.

Bring the list to the gate with a recommendation on what to cut. Marketing teams add
tags by default and nobody ever removes one; this is the only moment in the project
where the whole list is visible at once.

### The performance budget

Declare it, per `§19`:

- **Shell** — HTML, CSS, fonts, critical JS. Under 100KB. Paints something real alone.
  LCP under 2.0s on a throttled mid-range Android, targeting 1.5s
- **Heavy layer** — shaders, 3D, video, physics. Lazy-loaded after first paint, gated
  on intersection, never in the LCP path. State the number
- **Third-party** — the total from the tag list, with its own number

A technique that cannot be deferred has to justify its bytes at this gate, in front of
the client, against the conversion goal.

### Write `DIRECTION.md`

Concept and why it won. The collision, and which parent is structural. Palette with
hexes, sampled sources, and contrast results. Type system and licensing. Per-template
technique assignment. Motion spec. All three budget tiers. The tag list with owners.
**What was invented** — the thing that exists in this run and no other (`§3`).

> ## Gate B2 — human decision
>
> Show the prototype screenshots, the motion spec, the three-tier budget, and the tag
> list. They approve the technique set or cut what does not earn its place, and they
> approve or cut each tag with its owner named.
>
> This is the last stop before real code.

### When B2 rejects

Cut the technique, or swap it for another from `CRAFT.md`, then re-prototype. A
rejected prototype never gets argued into acceptance, tuned during the build, or
carried forward on the theory that it comes together in integration.

is a valid outcome — the section ships in its base state and the budget improves.

what they reacted against, and what that says about the ICP, the buyer's risk
appetite, or the positioning that `BRIEF.md` failed to capture. Recording only the
correction throws away the more valuable half.

|---|---|
| 2a design images | Seeing it before it is built. You iterate in code instead: slower, and biased toward whatever got built first |
| Gate B1 | The concept choice. You pick; they see it at Gate C, which is a late place to discover a disagreement |
| 2b prototypes | Proof the technique works before the design depends on it. Late failures are expensive |
| 2b tag list | The only moment the whole third-party list is visible at once. Tags get added later with no owner and no budget |
| Gate B2 | Motion review, and the performance budget goes undeclared |

# Loop 3 — Copy

**Goal:** every string that will appear on the site, written in the customer's words,
mapped to the message hierarchy, with every factual claim checked against
`EVIDENCE.md`.

**Input:** `BRIEF.md` (message hierarchy, objection ladder, VOC extract, voice),
`EVIDENCE.md`, `DIRECTION.md` (so the copy fits the design that exists).

**Output:** `COPY.md`.

---

## Why this comes before Build

Design built around placeholder text breaks when real text arrives. A hero designed
for six words gets a fourteen-word headline, a feature card designed for two lines
gets five, and the fix is either worse copy or a redesign — and under deadline it is
always worse copy.

On a marketing site this matters more than anywhere else, because **the copy is the
product.** A visitor does not experience the layout; they read a sentence and decide.
Design serves that sentence.

## The rule that governs this loop

`§5`: **write in the customer's words, not the company's.** The VOC extract in
`BRIEF.md` is not decoration. Open it, and use those phrases for problems, symptoms,
and outcomes. The company register from `POSITIONING.md §11` governs tone; the
customer lexicon governs nouns and verbs.

The single most common failure: a hero line describing what the software *is*, in the
vocabulary of the roadmap, to a visitor who came looking for a solution to a symptom.

## The headline

Top-tier work, and the conductor writes it rather than a worker. It is one line
carrying the positioning, the customer's language, and the top objection at once, and
it is the highest-leverage sentence on the site.

Write at least eight. Then test each against four checks:

| Check | Fails when |
|---|---|
| **Substitution** | A named competitor could put their name on it and it stays true |
| **Category** | A visitor cannot tell what kind of thing this is |
| **Language** | The main noun or verb came from the roadmap, not the VOC file |
| **Forwarding** | The champion cannot paste it into Slack and have it make sense alone |

Bring three survivors to the client, not one. And note: the best headline is often a
customer's sentence with two words removed.

## Page by page

Dispatch `page-writer`, one agent per page, in parallel. Each writes to the message
hierarchy and to the approved design image, and each checks every claim against
`EVIDENCE.md`.

Every page states, at the top of its section in `COPY.md`:

- **The one job** — the single action it exists to cause (`§7`)
- **Who lands here**, and from where
- **Which hierarchy levels it carries**
- **Which objections it answers**, in order

### The home page

Routes rather than explains. Its job is to make the right visitor go one level deeper,
not to say everything. The most common failure is a home page trying to be the product
page, the about page, and the pricing page at once.

Structure follows the objection ladder, not convention. If the top objection is trust,
proof comes before features. If it is fit, the vertical evidence comes before
anything.

### Product and service pages

One per genuinely distinct offering. Lead with the outcome in the customer's words,
then the mechanism, then the proof. Features are the third thing on the page, never
the first — a feature list answers "what is it" for someone who has already decided
they want it.

Show the product (`§11`). The copy's job is to frame the screenshot, not to substitute
for it.

### Pricing

Per `CONVERSION.md §5`. Tiers named for who they are for. The recommended one
obviously recommended, with an honest reason. Every inclusion claim checked (`§6`) —
"unlimited" had better be unlimited. An FAQ under the table answering overages, seats,
notice period, and what happens to the data if they leave.

### Case studies

Five beats, and the fourth is the one everyone cuts:

**Problem** — what was wrong before, in the customer's words
**Constraint** — what made it hard, and why the obvious fix did not work
**Decision** — the call, and what it gave up
**What broke** — the thing that went wrong. Keep this beat
**Outcome** — sourced, dated, ranked (`§6`)

Named customer, named person, real numbers, cleared (`§25`). The customer's own words
wherever you have them. A case study with no friction in it reads as marketing,
because it is.

Under NDA: write the class of problem instead of the instance. "A payments platform
processing nine figures a year" carries the weight; the logo does not. Anonymized
still has to be true, and it traces to `EVIDENCE.md` exactly as a named claim does.

### Comparison pages

The highest-value page most sites do not have, and the highest-risk one
(`COMPLIANCE.md §2`). Every claim about the competitor sourced, dated, and linked to
their own material. Compare on dimensions a buyer weighs. **Say where they are
genuinely better** — a table where one column wins every row is read as marketing
rather than information, and it converts worse for exactly that reason.

### About

Answers the trust objection, and on an agency site it is frequently the second most
visited page. Real people with real names and real photographs (`§25` — never
generated). What the company is for, what it refuses, who is accountable. Not a
founding-myth paragraph about a problem the founders noticed.

### The small print

Nav labels, buttons, form labels and help text, validation errors in plain words,
empty states, the success state, the autoresponder email, the 404 page, the footer,
and the legal pages' plain-language summaries. This is where sites reveal whether
anyone was paying attention.

Error messages are copy. "Something went wrong" is an unwritten string.

## Objections, placed

`§9`: place the answer where the objection occurs, not collected in a bottom FAQ.

Walk the objection ladder from `BRIEF.md` and assign each one a location in a specific
page at a specific point. The `COPY.md` template has a table for it. An objection with
no location assigned has not been answered — it has been listed.

An FAQ section is still useful for the long tail and for search. It is not where the
top three objections live.

## Calls to action

Per `CONVERSION.md §3`. Say what happens, not what to do. State the cost next to the
ask. One primary per page. Never "Submit".

Write the microcopy under the button too — "No card. Two minutes." removes the
objection at the exact point of decision, and it is three words.

## The prose pass

Three passes, in order, on everything:

1. **`stop-slop`** — strip the AI tells: the "not X, but Y" contrast, the em-dash tic,
   the reflexive three-item list, the hollow superlative (`§20`)
2. **`copywriting`** — clarity, specificity, rhythm, the promise in the first line
3. **`ogilvy`** — does it sell, and would the reader act

Then read it aloud. Anything you stumble on is a sentence a visitor will skim.

Note in `COPY.md` anything the passes changed materially — it is a useful signal about
whether the source material was thin.

## The evidence check

Before `COPY.md` is done, cross-reference every factual statement against
`EVIDENCE.md` (`§6`, hard):

- Every number has a source and a date
- Every superlative has substantiation, or it is cut
- Every comparison links to the competitor's own material
- Every testimonial has an approval on file
- Every logo has a written permission (`§25`)
- Every certification claim matches an actual certificate — "in progress" is never
  "compliant"

Anything failing goes back to the client as a question, not out as a silent cut. They
frequently have the source and did not know you needed it.

## Reading level and length

Write for the person who will forward this, on a phone, between meetings. Short
sentences. The claim first, the qualification second. No paragraph over four lines on
mobile.

Length follows the decision, not a rule: a £40k contract needs more page than a £19
subscription, and both need every line to earn its place. Cut anything that does not
map to a hierarchy level.

## Localization

If the site ships in more than one language (`§26`), copy is written per locale, not
translated at the end. A translated hero with an English CTA is worse than an English
site. Number and date formats, name order, and address shapes are copy decisions too.

## Skip cost

Skipping copy means the design gets built around placeholder lengths and then breaks,
and the client writes the words at the last minute in their own vocabulary — which
undoes `§5` and most of Loop 1 with it.

Skipping the objection mapping means the answers collect in a bottom FAQ, where
objections go to be ignored.

Skipping the evidence check is not available (`§6`).

# Loop 4 — Build

**Goal:** the site exists, coded to the approved images, with real copy in it, in all
three states, under budget, and editable by the client.

**Input:** `DIRECTION.md`, the design images, `COPY.md`, the prototypes.

**Output:** the site, in the client's repository.

---

## Stack

Settled at Gate A (`ARCHITECTURE.md`). Default is hand-authored HTML and CSS with
committed assets — it runs on all nine deploy targets and it is the fastest thing that
can be built. A publishing cadence moves it to a generator; a non-technical editor
moves it to a CMS.

**Do not ship a framework to the browser for a marketing site.** It is the most common
reason a company site fails Core Web Vitals, and Core Web Vitals are a ranking input
(`§19`). A generator that outputs static HTML is a build-time tool and is fine.

## The shell contract, first

Before any page is built, one person builds the shell and everything else consumes it.
Parallel page builds that each invent their own spacing scale produce a site that
looks assembled, which is exactly what this pipeline exists to avoid.

The shell owns:

### The token file

One file. Every value in it, nothing hardcoded anywhere else.

- Color: substrate, surfaces, text ramp, accent, and the full state set — error,
  success, warning, focus, disabled. Both modes, art-directed separately
- Type: families, the scale, line heights, measures, and the separate mobile scale
- Space: one scale, used everywhere
- Radius, border, shadow: the small set the design actually uses
- Motion: durations and easings from the motion spec, and the reduced-motion values
- Breakpoints and container widths
- Z-index: a named ladder, so the sticky CTA and the cookie banner and the nav do not
  fight in production

### The head

Charset, viewport, title and description per page, canonical, OG and Twitter tags,
favicon set, theme-color, preloads for the LCP image and any font in the LCP element,
and the JSON-LD block. Loop 5 fills the per-page values; the shape lives here.

### The frame

Skip link, header, nav, footer, and the `§27` attribution. Keyboard reachable, current
page indicated, works at 360px, and present on every page including the deepest post.

### The primitives

Buttons, links, form fields, labels, help text, error and success states, tables,
cards, and the section wrapper. Every one with hover, focus-visible, active, and
disabled states designed rather than defaulted.

Build the form primitives properly here, once. They are the `§18` surface and every
page reuses them.

## Fan out

Dispatch `page-builder`, one agent per page, each in its own git worktree so parallel
builds do not collide. Each agent codes **its page only** — never the shell, never the
tokens, never another page's section.

Give each one: its design image, its copy from `COPY.md`, the shell contract, the
technique assignment from `DIRECTION.md`, and the prototype for that technique.

When an agent finds a spec ambiguity, it reports rather than deciding. A builder
inventing a spacing value is how a design system quietly gets a second one.

## Code to the image

The approved design image is the spec. Match the composition, the type scale, the
spacing rhythm, the crop, and the color. Where the image and the copy disagree —
because real copy is longer than the render assumed — the copy wins and the layout
adapts. Note it, so the pattern shows up if it repeats.

Do not redesign during the build. If the image is wrong, that goes back to the
conductor, not into the code.

## Responsive

Three widths minimum, real designs at each: 360, 768, 1440. Not one design that
shrinks.

- **Mobile first, actually.** Most B2B traffic is now mobile, including the buying
  committee's first look, and the champion frequently forwards a link that gets opened
  on a phone
- Fluid type with clamps, and a separate mobile type scale where the display sizes
  need one
- Container queries for components living in more than one context
- Test at 320px and at 200% zoom — both are `§17` requirements and both break
  display-scale typography
- Tables get a real mobile design, not a horizontal scroll of the desktop table
- The primary CTA is reachable on mobile without hunting. A sticky ask is allowed if
  it does not cover the content that argues for it

## Images and media

- Modern formats with fallbacks, `srcset` and `sizes` real rather than decorative
- Explicit `width` and `height` on everything, always. Layout shift after paint is a
  Core Web Vitals failure and the cheapest one to avoid
- LCP image preloaded, correctly sized, never lazy-loaded
- Everything below the fold lazy
- Descriptive `alt` on every image (`§17`), meaningful filenames (`SEO.md`)
- Video: poster image in the shell, player loaded on interaction, never autoplay with
  sound, captions on anything with speech
- Product screenshots at the resolution that makes the UI legible — a blurred
  dashboard is worse than no dashboard (`§11`)

## The three states, per section

Every technique, every time (`§17`):

| State | What ships |
|---|---|
| **Full** | The designed experience |
| **Reduced motion** | An art-directed still. A composed frame someone designed, never `animation: none` |
| **Fallback** | No WebGL, no JS, blocked scripts, old GPU. A real page, never an apology |

The fallback matters commercially here: the visitor on locked-down corporate hardware
is frequently the enterprise buyer.

## Forms

Built here, wired in Loop 5. Per `CONVERSION.md §4`:

- Semantic markup, visible associated labels, correct `type` and `autocomplete`
- Validate on blur, errors next to the field in words, announced to assistive tech
- **Never clear the form on error.** Never lose what they typed
- Submit disabled only while in flight, with a changed label
- Real success state on the page, saying what happens next and when
- Failure state with a route out — an email address to write to instead
- Honeypot and a time-to-submit threshold (`CONVERSION.md §4`)
- It works with JavaScript disabled, or it degrades to a `mailto:` that at least tells
  the visitor the truth

## Vendor everything (`§14`)

Before the build is done: every library, font, and icon downloaded, committed, and
served from the client's own origin. No CDN in production. Pin versions. Keep the
licenses in the repo (`COMPLIANCE.md §3`).

Prototypes were allowed to pull from anywhere. That freedom ends here.

## Third-party tags

Only the ones approved at Gate B2, each loaded after consent (`§16`) and after first
paint (`§15`). None of them in the LCP path. Reserve space for anything that injects
into the layout, including the cookie banner — a banner that shifts the page after
paint is a CLS failure the compliance team mandated and nobody measured.

## Editability

Whatever was decided at Gate A (`ARCHITECTURE.md`), build it now rather than
retrofitting:

- Content collections with typed frontmatter, if a generator
- CMS schema with typed fields — heading, body, image with **required** alt text — and
  no way to set a color or a font size
- Preview before publish, drafts that do not leak into RSS or the sitemap
- A build that cannot deploy a broken page

**Output:** the site, in the client's repository.

---

## Stack

Settled at Gate A (`ARCHITECTURE.md`). Default is hand-authored HTML and CSS with
committed assets — it runs on all nine deploy targets and it is the fastest thing that
can be built. A publishing cadence moves it to a generator; a non-technical editor
moves it to a CMS.

**Do not ship a framework to the browser for a marketing site.** It is the most common
reason a company site fails Core Web Vitals, and Core Web Vitals are a ranking input
(`§19`). A generator that outputs static HTML is a build-time tool and is fine.

## The shell contract, first

Before any page is built, one person builds the shell and everything else consumes it.
Parallel page builds that each invent their own spacing scale produce a site that
looks assembled, which is exactly what this pipeline exists to avoid.

The shell owns:

### The token file

One file. Every value in it, nothing hardcoded anywhere else.

- Color: substrate, surfaces, text ramp, accent, and the full state set — error,
  success, warning, focus, disabled. Both modes, art-directed separately
- Type: families, the scale, line heights, measures, and the separate mobile scale
- Space: one scale, used everywhere
- Radius, border, shadow: the small set the design actually uses
- Motion: durations and easings from the motion spec, and the reduced-motion values
- Breakpoints and container widths
- Z-index: a named ladder, so the sticky CTA and the cookie banner and the nav do not
  fight in production

### The head

Charset, viewport, title and description per page, canonical, OG and Twitter tags,
favicon set, theme-color, preloads for the LCP image and any font in the LCP element,
and the JSON-LD block. Loop 5 fills the per-page values; the shape lives here.

### The frame

Skip link, header, nav, footer, and the `§27` attribution. Keyboard reachable, current
page indicated, works at 360px, and present on every page including the deepest post.

### The primitives

cards, and the section wrapper. Every one with hover, focus-visible, active, and
disabled states designed rather than defaulted.

page reuses them.

tokens, never another page's section.

technique assignment from `DIRECTION.md`, and the prototype for that technique.

inventing a spacing value is how a design system quietly gets a second one.

The approved design image is the spec. Match the composition, the type scale, the

# Loop 5 — Capture & Convert

**Goal:** the site can be found, can be shared, can receive a lead and deliver it to a
human, and can report on itself.

**Input:** the built site, `BRIEF.md`, `DIRECTION.md`, `redirects.csv`.

**Output:** `FUNNEL.md`, and a site that is wired rather than decorative.

---

## Why this exists as its own loop

The build produces something that looks finished. This loop is everything that makes
it work, and it is the half that gets rushed because it is invisible in a screenshot.

Three of the six hard rules land here: consent before tracking (`§16`), the conversion
path proven end to end (`§18`, verified in Loop 7), and the redirect map applied
(`§13`).

---

## 1. The forms, wired

Per `CONVERSION.md §4`. The markup was built in Loop 4; this is where it goes
somewhere.

- Endpoint decided at Gate A: CRM, transactional email, channel, database, or a form
  service
- Server-side validation as well as client-side. Never trust the browser
- Server-side rate limit, plus the honeypot and time threshold from Loop 4
- The submission is stored durably **and** notified. A channel message alone is not a
  record; a database row alone is not a notification
- Autoresponder that confirms receipt and names the response time
- UTM and referrer captured with the lead, so attribution survives to the CRM
- Field mapping written down in `FUNNEL.md`, including which field routes the lead

### Email deliverability

If anything sends mail from the client's domain, set SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. This is a
deliverability requirement now, not a nicety. A confirmation email landing in spam is
an `§18` failure the client cannot see, and it looks exactly like a working site.

Never use the host's `mail()`. Use a transactional provider with a verified sending
domain.

### Booking and calendar links

If the offer is a booked slot: the calendar is embedded or linked, availability is
real, the confirmation says what happens next, and a booking fires the conversion
event once. Test a real booking and then cancel it.

## 2. Consent, before anything tracks (`§16`, hard)

Configure this **before** the tags, not after.

- Nothing fires before consent where consent is required, and the safe default is that
  it is required
- Scripts are blocked from loading, not merely told not to report
- Reject is exactly as easy as accept: one click, same level, same weight
- Per-purpose choices, nothing pre-ticked, no consent inferred from scrolling
- Withdrawable later from a persistent control
- The choice is stored and honored on the next visit
- Space reserved in the layout so it does not shift the page after paint (`§19`)

Prefer the route with no banner at all: cookieless, aggregate analytics with no
cross-site identifier. Fewer banners, faster page, and better data, because consent
rates mean a cookie-based setup is missing a large share of sessions anyway.

Whatever is chosen, the cookie notice lists what is actually set, and the privacy
notice is true about what actually happens to a form submission
([`COMPLIANCE.md`](../COMPLIANCE.md)).

## 3. Analytics and events

Per [`MEASURE.md`](../MEASURE.md). One property, not three.

Install the event model — `page_view`, `cta_click`, `form_start`, `form_submit`,
`form_error`, `conversion`, and whatever else the funnel needs. Rules that matter more
than the choice of tool:

- **Fire once.** A conversion double-firing on a re-render corrupts the number and
  costs money on ad platforms
- **Only on success.** A `form_submit` fired on button click counts every failure as a
  win, which means a completely broken form reports perfect conversion
- **`form_error` with a reason.** The most under-collected and most useful event
  available
- Named consistently, documented in `FUNNEL.md` with trigger and properties

Also: Search Console verified and the sitemap submitted, one uptime check, and an
alert if zero form submissions arrive in N days — the cheapest insurance in the
pipeline against the silent `§18` failure.

## 4. SEO technical layer

Per [`SEO.md`](../SEO.md). The content work happened in Loops 1 and 3; this is the
plumbing.

- **`robots.txt`** allowing what should be crawled. Check the built output — a staging
  `Disallow: /` shipped to production is the most common catastrophic launch bug, and
  it is silent
- **No `noindex` in production.** Again, check the output, not the template
- **Sitemap** of live, canonical, indexable URLs only. Referenced from `robots.txt`
- **Canonicals** self-referential and absolute
- **Titles and descriptions** unique per page, within length, written for the click
- **The redirect map applied** (`§13`) — in the adapter's config, single hop, 301
- **One hostname, one protocol, one trailing-slash rule**, everything else redirecting
  to it in a single hop
- **`hreflang`** on every locale variant with a self-reference and `x-default`, if
  multilingual

## 5. Structured data

JSON-LD in the head, validated, and only types that are true of the page:
`Organization` and `WebSite` on home, `BreadcrumbList` below the top level,
`Product` or `SoftwareApplication` on product pages, `Article` on posts with real
dates and a real author, `FAQPage` only where visible FAQ content exists,
`LocalBusiness` only for real locations matching the business listing.

Never mark up content that is not visible on the page.

## 6. The share layer

The champion pastes the link into Slack before anyone visits the site. That preview is
the buying committee's first impression, and it arrives before the page loads.

- **OG image**, 1200×630, under 300KB, in the design system, with the message on it.
  Per page for anything worth forwarding on its own — a case study that unfurls as the
  homepage wastes the click
- Generated at build time from the page title where volume justifies it: one template,
  N images, no manual work per post
- `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:url`, `og:type`, `twitter:card`, all per page
- Favicons: the full set, including a maskable icon and `theme-color` for both modes
- Test the actual unfurl in a real client. The tags being present is not the same as
  the preview rendering

## 7. Legal pages

Per [`COMPLIANCE.md`](../COMPLIANCE.md), driven by the markets named at intake:
privacy notice, cookie notice, terms if transactional, imprint where required,
company details in the footer where required, an accessibility statement, and a
working route for a data request.

The privacy notice has to be true about what this site actually does. A generated
template that mentions services the site does not use is worse than a short honest
one.

## 8. Performance, verified against the budget

The heavy layer is deferred and outside the LCP path. Third-party tags are within
their Gate B2 number and load after consent and after first paint. The hero image is
preloaded and sized. Fonts are subset and preloaded only where they are in the LCP
element. Nothing shifts after paint.

Measure on a throttled mid-range Android. If the budget is blown, the fix is cutting
something, and the tag list is the first place to look — not the design.

## 9. The 404 and the empty states

A real 404 page in the design system, with a route back to the pages that matter. It
gets more traffic than anyone expects, especially after a migration.

Empty and error states for anything dynamic: search with no results, a form that
failed, a live data panel whose source is down. Each one is copy that Loop 3 should
have written; if it did not, write it now rather than shipping "Something went wrong".

## Write `FUNNEL.md`

The document Loop 7 verifies against and Loop 8 reads:

- The path, step by step, from source to sale
- Every form: fields, endpoint, destination, who reads it, field mapping
- Every event: name, trigger, properties, where it fires
- The consent configuration: what is blocked before consent, what fires after
- The tag list from Gate B2, with owners
- The conversion definition — what counts, and what does not
- The UTM convention
- The dashboard link, and who has access

## Skip costs

| Skipping | Costs |
|---|---|
| Forms wiring | `§18`. Not available in substance — a site that cannot receive a lead is not finished |
| CRM integration | Leads land in an inbox someone must remember to check. Acceptable only if that person is named |
| Consent config | `§16`. Not available where consent is required |
| Analytics and events | Loop 8, and any ability to say whether the run worked |
| SEO technical layer | Indexing problems that surface weeks later, and the redirect map unapplied (`§13`) |
| Structured data | Rich results and some free credibility in the results page |
| Share layer | The unfurl. The first impression the buying committee gets. Cheapest step in the pipeline to keep |
| Legal pages | A legal requirement wherever a form exists ([`COMPLIANCE.md`](../COMPLIANCE.md)) |
| 404 and empty states | The visitor who hits one, which after a migration is more people than the client expects |

# Loop 6 — Deploy

**Goal:** the site is live on the client's infrastructure, on their accounts, with the
redirects in place and a rollback that works.

**Input:** the built and wired site, `redirects.csv`, the target from Gate A.

**Output:** a live URL, a snapshot, a documented rollback, and a handover the client
has used.

---

## The conductor runs this. Never delegate it.

It holds credentials and it is the irreversible one. Subagents do not deploy, do not
touch DNS, and do not hold secrets.

## Gate C comes first — never skipped (`§22`)

Nothing becomes publicly visible on a company's domain before the person accountable
has seen it.

> ## Gate C — human decision
>

# Loop 7 — Verify

**Goal:** confirm with your eyes and with a real submission that the live site renders,
ranks, and converts. Then write down honestly what this run produced.

**Input:** the live URL, `FUNNEL.md`, `redirects.csv`, `SKIPS.md`.

**Output:** `runs/<slug>/REPORT.md` with a confidence grade, and `shots/live/`.

---

## Verify the live URL, never the local build

Local and live differ in ways that matter: absolute paths, MIME types, compression,
cache headers, TLS, redirects, and whatever the host rewrites. `HTTP 200` is not "it
renders", and a form that worked locally can post to nowhere in production.

Two agents run in parallel: `site-verifier` for the checklist, `funnel-verifier` for
the conversion path. The conductor looks at the screenshots afterward, because an
automated pass and a page that looks wrong are compatible states.

## The checklist — 24 checks

### Renders

1. **360 / 768 / 1440**, every template. Nothing overflows, collapses, or overlaps.
   Screenshot each into `shots/live/`
2. **Both color modes.** Both designed. Neither an inversion artifact
3. **Reduced motion.** Forced on, still a designed page
4. **Fallback.** Block WebGL and block JS. The page still carries its content
5. **320px and 200% zoom.** Both `§17` requirements, both break display type

### Accessible (`§17`, hard)

6. **Keyboard.** Tab everything, including the form and any modal. Visible focus, no
   traps, skip link works, focus returns after a dialog closes
7. **axe.** Zero violations, not zero criticals
8. **Contrast.** Body text at 4.5:1 measured on the live render, including over
   imagery, translucency, and after any grade or grain
9. **Alt text.** Every image, descriptive, never a filename
10. **Forms.** Labels associated, errors announced and linked to their field, no
    color-only signaling

### Fast (`§19`)

11. **Lighthouse mobile.** Record all four scores
12. **Core Web Vitals** on a throttled mid-range profile: LCP, INP, CLS against the
    Gate B2 budget
13. **Shell budget.** Under 100KB, heavy layer deferred and out of the LCP path
14. **No layout shift after paint**, cookie banner included
15. **Console.** Zero errors on load and after a full scroll

### Found (`§13`, `SEO.md`)

16. **`robots.txt`** allows what should be crawled, and there is no production
    `noindex`. Check the live output, not the template
17. **Sitemap** lists live canonical URLs only, and is referenced from `robots.txt`
18. **One hostname, one protocol, one trailing-slash rule.** `http` redirects, apex
    and `www` resolve deliberately, single hop
19. **Redirects.** Sample the map, and verify **all** of the top-20-by-traffic rows.
    301, single hop, correct target
20. **Meta.** Titles and descriptions unique, present, in length. One `h1` per page,
    heading order intact. Canonicals absolute and self-referential
21. **Structured data** validates and matches visible content

### Converts (`§18`, hard)

22. **The funnel, end to end.** Run by `funnel-verifier`, and it is the check this
    loop exists for. See below
23. **Unfurl.** Paste the URL into a real client and look at the preview. Tags being
    present is not the preview rendering
24. **Every link.** Click all of them. Zero 404s, zero dead anchors, outbound links go
    where they claim

### Concrete starting points

```bash
mkdir -p runs/<slug>/shots/live
for w in 360 768 1440; do
  chrome --headless --window-size=$w,1400 --screenshot=runs/<slug>/shots/live/$w.png "<live-url>"
done
npx @axe-core/cli "<live-url>"
npx lighthouse "<live-url>" --preset=desktop --output=json --output-path=runs/<slug>/lh-desktop.json --quiet
npx lighthouse "<live-url>" --output=json --output-path=runs/<slug>/lh-mobile.json --quiet
npx lychee --no-progress "<live-url>"
curl -sI "https://<domain>" | head -20
curl -s "https://<domain>/robots.txt"
```

## The funnel proof (`§18`, hard)

`funnel-verifier` runs all of it, live, per [`MEASURE.md`](../MEASURE.md) §4:

1. Load with consent **rejected**. Confirm no analytics request goes out (`§16`)
2. Accept. Confirm exactly one `page_view`
3. Click the primary CTA. Confirm one `cta_click` with the right location property
4. Focus the form. Confirm one `form_start`
5. **Submit a real, clearly labeled test lead**
6. Confirm the success state renders, and `form_submit` fires **once**
7. Confirm the lead arrives at every destination: CRM record, inbox, channel
8. Confirm the autoresponder sends, and check it did not land in spam
9. Confirm the conversion appears in the analytics property, not just the network tab
10. Repeat on mobile and in the second-most-used browser
11. Trigger a validation error deliberately; confirm `form_error` fires with a reason
12. Delete or label the test lead so sales does not call it

**Steps 7 and 8 cannot be completed from a browser.** The agent reports them as
partial and the conductor confirms the far end with the client. An agent watching a
success message is not evidence a lead arrived, and claiming otherwise is the exact
failure `§18` exists to prevent.

Booking flow instead of a form? Book a real slot, confirm it appears on the calendar,
confirm the confirmation email, then cancel it.

## Then look at the screenshots yourself

The conductor does this, not an agent. Open every shot in `shots/live/` and look.
Automated checks pass on pages that are visibly wrong: a hero cropped at 768, a nav
that wraps into two lines, a CTA below the fold on a laptop, a product screenshot too
small to read.

## Handle failures

Fix what is fixable now, re-verify, and record both states. Log the rest with what it
would take to fix. **Never report a fix you did not confirm**, and never paper over a
failure with a caveat. If check 7 found axe violations, that goes on the first page of
the report, not in a footnote.

Two failures stop everything and get fixed before the run continues:

- A production `noindex` or a `Disallow: /` — the site is invisible and nobody will
  notice for weeks
- A form that does not deliver — the site looks fine and every lead is falling on the
  floor

## The report

`runs/<slug>/REPORT.md` opens with the grade and its reason, then the failures, then
everything else.

| Grade | Means |
|---|---|
| **A** | Full pipeline. Claims substantiated, positioning derived from real market and customer evidence, design validated at both gates, funnel proven live, instrumented and measurable |
| **B** | Core intact, some validation skipped. Strategy or design review thinner than ideal. Everything hard still held |
| **C** | Substance skipped — no VOC, no competitor work, or no real copy pass. A good-looking site making the client's own claims in the client's own words |
| **D** | Multiple substance skips, or shipped without measurement. A redesign whose effect nobody will ever know. Say exactly that |

Read `SKIPS.md` and grade against it. A **D** stated plainly is more useful than an
**A** claimed falsely.

Then: the live URL, all 24 checks with results, the screenshots, the Lighthouse and
CWV numbers, the funnel proof with the two partial steps flagged, the redirect
verification, what was skipped and what it cost, the rollback command, every claim you
flagged that the client overruled (`COMPLIANCE.md §8`), the baseline for Loop 8, and
what would move the grade up.

## Schedule Loop 8

Before closing this loop, agree the date. Two weeks minimum for a directional read,
four to six for anything actionable, longer on a low-traffic B2B site. Put it in the
report. A launch with no scheduled read is a launch nobody learns from.

## Skip cost

Skipping verification means the first person to find the broken form is a customer, and
the first person to notice the `noindex` is whoever wonders why traffic went to zero.

Skipping the funnel proof is not available (`§18`).
